findings.verifierNote: experiments.ts:54 is verbatim, the cache is an in-memory Map, and the engine has no import or field referencing AnalyticsCollector or any transport — the missing exposure event and the missing traffic-allocation/holdout/kill-switch features are real gaps. But the primary framing is partly refuted: recomputation is the documented and intended design ('deterministic ... no server round-trip required', experiments.ts:4-6; guide/analytics.md:65), and it delivers stickiness for a fixed experiment definition, so 'recomputed rather than persisted' is by design, not a bug. The genuine defect is the re-bucketing on any weight/variant change plus the absent exposure event, which is a notable gap rather than a serious missing-implementation.

findings.title: No transport propagates userId to the provider's identity field, so tour events attach to anonymous device ids
findings.impact: `CollectorOptions.userId` becomes an ordinary property named `user_id` (collector.ts:108). PostHog attributes events by `distinct_id`, Mixpanel by `distinct_id`, Amplitude by `eventOptions.user_id` — none of them read a property called `user_id`. So if the host app has not independently called `posthog.identify()`/`mixpanel.identify()`, every tour event lands on the anonymous device profile even though the collector was explicitly given a real user id, and cohorting tour completion against account attributes is impossible. No transport exposes `identify()`, user properties, super properties, or group/company analytics, and there is no way to update `userId` on the collector after construction (`opts` is set once at line 40, no setter), so a login mid-session leaves the rest of the session mis-attributed. Separately, the `$timestamp` property here is dead weight: `$`-prefixed names are PostHog-reserved, and the declared global type `capture: (event: string, props?: Record<string, unknown>) => void` (line 6) has no third parameter, so the transport structurally cannot pass posthog-js's real `options.timestamp` override — every event is stamped at ingestion time, which matters precisely for the batched/unload path.
findings.fix: Add an optional `identify(userId, traits?)` to `AnalyticsTransport` and `AnalyticsCollector.identify()`/`setUserId()`, and implement it per provider (`posthog.identify`, `mixpanel.identify` + `people.set`, `amplitude.setUserId`, `analytics.identify`). Widen the declared global signatures to include the third options argument and pass the real timestamp override (`{ timestamp: new Date(event.timestamp) }` for PostHog).
findings.verifierNote: posthog.ts:18-25 sends only a properties bag; collector.ts:108 puts the id under the ordinary key user_id, which none of PostHog/Mixpanel/Amplitude read as identity. opts is assigned once at collector.ts:40 with no setter, so userId cannot be updated mid-session. The $timestamp point checks out too: the declared global at posthog.ts:5-7 is `capture: (event, props?) => void`, with no third options parameter, so the real timestamp override is structurally unreachable. Severity corrected: all four transports already require the vendor SDK to be initialised on the page (transports.md:22,36,50,64), and initialisation in practice includes the host app's own identify() call, so the mis-attribution is conditional rather than universal.

findings.title: Mixpanel and Amplitude transports pass an ISO-8601 string in `time`, where both SDKs expect a numeric epoch
findings.impact: `event.timestamp` is `new Date().toISOString()` (collector.ts:105). Mixpanel's reserved `time` property must be a numeric UNIX timestamp; a string is not parsed as the event time, so the intended backdating silently fails and the event is stamped at ingestion. amplitude.ts:18 is identical, and Amplitude's Browser SDK 2.x takes the event time as `eventOptions.time` (epoch ms) in a third argument that the declared global type `track: (event: string, props?: Record<string, unknown>) => void` (amplitude.ts:6) cannot express. The practical impact lands on the batched/offline path: events queued during a 5-second batch window or replayed after a network outage are attributed to the wrong moment, corrupting time-on-step and session-stitching in exactly the analyses `dwell_ms` exists to support. Additionally, `window.amplitude.track` only exists in Amplitude Browser SDK 2.x; a consumer on `amplitude-js` v1 (where the API is `amplitude.getInstance().logEvent()`) has a truthy `window.amplitude` whose `.track` is undefined, so `track()` throws, the collector catches it (collector.ts:116) and logs `Transport "amplitude" threw:` for every event forever.
findings.fix: Widen each declared global signature to include the SDK's third options argument and pass the timestamp there (`mixpanel.track(name, props, {}, cb)` is not the path — use Mixpanel's numeric `time` property as `Date.parse(event.timestamp)`; for Amplitude pass `{ time: Date.parse(event.timestamp) }` as `eventOptions`). Feature-detect the method (`typeof window.amplitude?.track === 'function'`) rather than the object, and warn once with a version hint when the global exists but the method does not.
findings.verifierNote: mixpanel.ts:17-19 and amplitude.ts:17-19 both pass `time: event.timestamp`, and collector.ts:105 produces new Date().toISOString(). Mixpanel's reserved `time` is a numeric epoch and Amplitude 2.x takes event time via a third eventOptions argument that the declared globals (mixpanel.ts:6, amplitude.ts:6, both `(event, props?) => void`) cannot express. The amplitude-js v1 point also holds: window.amplitude would be truthy with .track undefined, throwing into the collector's catch at collector.ts:116 on every event.

findings.title: The failure counter is global, not per-batch, so a fresh batch can be dropped on its very first attempt
findings.impact: `_consecutiveFailures` is a transport-level counter that only resets on success (line 75) or on drop (line 88). Two unrelated transient failures spread over an hour leave it at 2; the next batch — containing brand-new events that have never been attempted — fails once, hits `2+1 < 3 === false`, and is discarded immediately. Second defect: the option is named `maxRetries` and documented as "Max consecutive flush failures before dropping the batch (default: 3)" (line 12), but the strict `<` means the default drops on the third *failure*, i.e. only 2 retries; `maxRetries: 1` drops on the first failure with zero retries, and `maxRetries: 0` disables retry entirely while reading as "no limit". Third defect: there is no backoff — with the default `batchIntervalMs: 0` a retry only happens when the next event arrives, so a queue can sit indefinitely on a low-traffic page, while on a busy page a dead endpoint is hammered once per event. Fourth: `this.queue.unshift(...batch)` spreads the batch as function arguments, which throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` once a batch grows past the engine's argument limit — reachable via the unbounded queue growth above.
findings.fix: Attach a per-batch `attempts` counter (wrap events in `{event, attempts}` or keep a parallel batch object) and drop only that batch when it exceeds `maxRetries`. Use `<=` or rename the option to `maxAttempts` and document the exact semantics. Add exponential backoff with jitter and schedule the retry on a timer rather than on the next `track()`. Replace `unshift(...batch)` with `this.queue = batch.concat(this.queue)`. Do not retry 4xx responses — inspect `response.status` and drop non-retryable client errors with a distinct warning.
findings.verifierNote: The counter is transport-scoped and only reset at :75 (success) and :88 (drop) — that part is confirmed. But the headline off-by-one sub-claim is wrong: the option is documented at webhook.ts:12 as 'Max consecutive flush failures before dropping the batch (default: 3)', and `_consecutiveFailures < 3` drops on exactly the 3rd consecutive failure, which matches the documented semantics precisely (only the name maxRetries is misleading). The 'two unrelated failures an hour apart' scenario also requires no intervening successful flush, since any success resets to 0 and a failed batch is re-queued and retried on the very next flush. The unshift(...batch) RangeError needs a batch of ~100k events, which the default maxQueueSize of 20 makes unreachable in practice, and is unreachable via the _flushing latch (flush never re-enters there). Real but narrower: global counter + no backoff.

findings.title: Four of five transports have zero tests, and one existing test asserts nothing
findings.evidence: "test": "vitest run --passWithNoTests",
findings.impact: `src/__tests__/` contains three files — collector, experiments, webhook. There is no test file for posthog.ts, mixpanel.ts, amplitude.ts or segment.ts, so the silent-drop-when-global-missing path (transports-silent-noop), the `$timestamp`/`time` mapping (provider-timestamp-format-wrong), and the throw-when-method-missing behaviour are all unverified — a rename of any window global would ship green. `--passWithNoTests` means deleting the test directory outright would not fail CI. Within the webhook suite, `it('destroy() clears the batch interval timer')` (src/__tests__/webhook.test.ts:114-118) contains no `expect` at all — its body is a comment reading "No way to directly assert timer cleared, but no errors = success" — so it passes unconditionally. The uncovered high-risk paths are precisely the ones this audit found broken: the `attach()` re-attach guard, the drop-after-maxRetries branch, the beforeunload flush, and the `_flushing` latch.
findings.fix: Add a `transports.test.ts` that stubs and un-stubs each window global and asserts both the delivered payload shape and the silent-drop path. Rewrite the destroy test with `vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` asserting no further `fetch` after `destroy()`, and add a `removeEventListener` spy. Add tests for attach-after-destroy, the maxRetries drop, and a never-resolving fetch. Drop `--passWithNoTests` from this package.
findings.verifierNote: packages/analytics/package.json:53 is exactly `"test": "vitest run --passWithNoTests",`. src/__tests__/ contains only collector.test.ts, experiments.test.ts and webhook.test.ts — no test for any of the four SDK transports. webhook.test.ts:114-118 is verbatim: the body is one comment, 'No way to directly assert timer cleared, but no errors = success', with no expect. I also confirmed collector.test.ts has no re-attach test (it covers detach() and the returned unsubscribe only, lines 130-141), so the attach guard is genuinely uncovered.

findings.title: All four SDK transports silently discard every event when the window global is absent — no warning, no buffering
findings.impact: Identical pattern in mixpanel.ts:16 (`window.mixpanel`), amplitude.ts:16 (`window.amplitude`), segment.ts:16 (`window.analytics`). If the global is missing the method returns `undefined` and the event is destroyed — no queue, no warning, no error, no counter. The realistic failure modes are all common and all silent: (1) the SDK snippet loads async and GuideFlow's first `tour.started` fires before it resolves, so the funnel's entry event is missing while later events arrive, permanently skewing completion rate above 100%-of-starts; (2) an ad blocker or a Brave/uBlock filter list blocks the vendor script, so a measurable slice of users report nothing at all; (3) a consent manager gates the SDK until acceptance; (4) a typo'd or renamed global. The class docstring at posthog.ts:12-13 actively markets this as a feature — "Lazy-accesses `window.posthog` so it works regardless of whether PostHog is loaded before or after GuideFlow" — but events emitted before load are dropped, not replayed. apps/docs/api/analytics/transports.md:22 only says the SDK must "already be initialised" and never mentions data loss.
findings.fix: Give each transport a bounded ring buffer (e.g. 50 events) used while the global is absent, drained on the next successful `track()` and on `flush()`. Emit one `console.warn` per transport the first time the global is missing, and expose an optional `onDropped(event, reason)` callback. Document the drop semantics in apps/docs/api/analytics/transports.md.
findings.verifierNote: posthog.ts:18-24 matches verbatim, and mixpanel.ts:16, amplitude.ts:16, segment.ts:16 are the identical `if (typeof window !== 'undefined' && window.X)` guard with no else branch, no queue and no warning. The marketing docstring is at posthog.ts:11-13 as quoted, and apps/docs/api/analytics/transports.md:22 only says the SDK must 'already be initialised'. Severity corrected: guarding on a missing vendor global is a common adapter pattern and warning per-event would be log spam; the defect is the total absence of any diagnostic or buffering, which is a notable gap rather than a serious shipped defect.

findings.title: WebhookTransport.destroy() is outside the AnalyticsTransport interface, so the collector never calls it and leaks a timer plus a beforeunload listener
findings.impact: `AnalyticsTransport` declares only `name`, `track` and optional `flush` (src/transports/interface.ts:15-28). `AnalyticsCollector` has `detach()` and `flush()` but no `destroy()`, and never touches transport lifecycle. Every `new WebhookTransport(...)` registers a `setInterval` (line 40) and a `beforeunload` listener (line 47) in its constructor and nothing in the package ever removes them. A React app that constructs a collector+transport per mount (or per route) accumulates one live interval and one live unload listener per instance, each holding a reference to its own queue — a compounding leak that also multiplies outbound requests. `destroy()` is invisible to TypeScript consumers who type the value as `AnalyticsTransport`, and it is not mentioned in apps/docs/api/analytics/transports.md at all. `destroy()` itself also calls `void this.flush()` without awaiting, so the final batch is fire-and-forget.
findings.fix: Add `destroy?(): void | Promise<void>` to `AnalyticsTransport`, add `AnalyticsCollector.destroy()` that detaches, awaits `flush()`, then awaits `destroy()` on every transport, and make `WebhookTransport.destroy()` async and await its final flush. Document `destroy()` in the transports reference and in the React/Vue/Svelte cleanup examples.
findings.verifierNote: transports/interface.ts:15-28 declares only name, track and optional flush — destroy is absent. webhook.ts constructor registers setInterval (:39-43) and beforeunload (:45-48); destroy() at :95-102 is the only cleanup and nothing in collector.ts references transport lifecycle (it has detach() and flush() only). transports.md never mentions destroy(). destroy() does call `void this.flush()` unawaited at :101. Severity corrected: destroy() is visible on the concrete `new WebhookTransport(...)` type (it is only hidden if the consumer widens to AnalyticsTransport), and the tests do call it, so this is a notable leak/API gap rather than a serious defect.

findings.title: ai/react/svelte/vue declare @guideflow/core as a runtime `dependency`, allowing two copies of core and breaking its instanceof check
findings.impact: README.md:57 tells users to `pnpm add @guideflow/core @guideflow/react`, so core is a direct dependency of the app. Because the adapter also declares it as a normal dependency (identically at packages/ai/package.json:58-60, packages/svelte:56-58, packages/vue:58-60), npm/yarn can and will install a second, differently-versioned copy under `node_modules/@guideflow/react/node_modules/@guideflow/core`. Both copies then evaluate, and packages/core/src/index.ts:178 (`if (renderer instanceof DefaultRenderer)`) silently returns false for a renderer built from the other copy — so `renderer.setActionHandler(...)` and `renderer.onInit(_config)` never run and the popover's next/prev/close buttons become inert. `@guideflow/analytics` already gets this right by using peerDependencies (packages/analytics/package.json:58-60), which makes the inconsistency plainly unintentional.
findings.fix: In packages/{ai,react,svelte,vue}/package.json move `@guideflow/core` out of `dependencies` into `peerDependencies` as `"@guideflow/core": "workspace:^"` and add it to `devDependencies` as `"workspace:*"` so local builds and type-checks still resolve. All four tsup configs already list `@guideflow/core` in `external`, so no build change is needed.
findings.verifierNote: The dependency facts are verbatim: react:57-59, ai:58-60, svelte:56-58, vue:58-60 all put @guideflow/core in `dependencies`, while analytics:58-60 uses peerDependencies — the inconsistency is real and duplicate-copy installs are a genuine risk. But the headline impact is wrong: packages/core/src/index.ts:161 creates `config.renderer ?? new DefaultRenderer()` from the same module copy that runs the line-178 `instanceof` check, so the guard passes in the default path. Breaking it requires a user to construct DefaultRenderer from copy A and hand it to createGuideFlow from copy B — a narrow case, not the described default failure of inert next/prev/close buttons.

findings.title: @guideflow/analytics lists @guideflow/core in peerDependencies as `workspace:*`, which publishes as an exact-version peer pin
findings.impact: I verified from the installed @changesets/cli that `changeset publish` shells out to `pnpm publish` when pnpm is the detected package manager, and pnpm rewrites the `workspace:` protocol on pack/publish across dependencies, devDependencies AND peerDependencies. `workspace:*` resolves to the *exact* current version, so the published manifest contains `"peerDependencies": { "@guideflow/core": "0.1.9" }`. Any consumer on core 0.1.10 — including anyone who follows README.md:76's `pnpm add @guideflow/analytics` after the next patch release — gets an unmet-peer error from pnpm/yarn (which fail hard) rather than a satisfied range. The duplicate `workspace:*` in devDependencies (line 62) is also published verbatim as `"0.1.9"`, adding noise to the manifest.
findings.fix: Change packages/analytics/package.json:59 to `"@guideflow/core": "workspace:^"` so it publishes as `^0.1.9`, and keep line 62's devDependencies entry as `"workspace:*"` (that one is correct for local resolution). Apply the same `workspace:^` form when converting ai/react/svelte/vue to peerDependencies.
findings.verifierNote: packages/analytics/package.json:58-62 matches verbatim — `peerDependencies: { "@guideflow/core": "workspace:*" }` immediately followed by the same spec in devDependencies at line 62. pnpm rewrites the workspace protocol on pack/publish across dependencies, devDependencies and peerDependencies alike, and `workspace:*` expands to the exact current version, so the published peer becomes `"0.1.9"`. Every sibling that uses `dependencies` has the same exact-pin behaviour, but only the peer form surfaces as an unmet-peer error to consumers.

findings.title: apps/e2e has no tsconfig.json, no @types/node and no window.__guideflow declaration — the suite can never be type-checked
findings.impact: apps/e2e is the only workspace with no tsconfig.json and no `type-check` or `lint` script, so Playwright's transpile-only esbuild pipeline is the only thing that ever reads these files — which is precisely why the non-existent `AxeBuilder` import (accessibility.spec.ts:2) survived. Two more errors are latent: apps/e2e/tests/tour-flow.spec.ts:13 references `window.__guideflow` with no global augmentation anywhere in apps/e2e, and apps/e2e/playwright.config.ts:6/:7/:8/:34 use `process.env` without `@types/node` being declared in the package. The .eslintrc.json resolver glob `apps/*/tsconfig.json` (.eslintrc.json:19) silently skips the directory.
findings.fix: Add apps/e2e/tsconfig.json extending ../../tsconfig.base.json with `"types": ["node"]` and `"include": ["tests", "playwright.config.ts", "types"]`, add `@types/node` to apps/e2e devDependencies, add `apps/e2e/types/global.d.ts` declaring `interface Window { __guideflow?: unknown }`, and add `"type-check": "tsc --noEmit"` plus `"lint": "eslint tests --max-warnings 0"` scripts so CI catches this class of error.
findings.verifierNote: apps/e2e/package.json:10-14 matches verbatim. A directory listing of apps/e2e shows only fixtures/, node_modules/, package.json, playwright.config.ts and tests/ — no tsconfig.json, and the manifest declares no type-check or lint script and no @types/node. tour-flow.spec.ts:13 does reference `window.__guideflow` with no global augmentation in the workspace, and playwright.config.ts uses process.env at lines 6, 7, 8 and 34. .eslintrc.json:19 is `"project": ["packages/*/tsconfig.json", "apps/*/tsconfig.json"]`, which cannot match a directory with no tsconfig. This is precisely why the phantom AxeBuilder import was never caught.

findings.title: CI runs one Node version, excludes all apps, and never runs e2e, size-limit, coverage or a changeset-presence check; the Turbo cache is not persisted
findings.evidence: run: pnpm turbo run build --filter=!storybook --filter=!docs --filter=!e2e --filter=!@guideflow/demo
findings.impact: The same four `--filter=!` exclusions are repeated on all four steps (lines 35, 38, 41, 44), so nothing in `apps/` is ever built, type-checked or linted by CI — apps/demo/src/App.tsx (400+ lines exercising every package) and apps/storybook/stories/TourFlow.stories.tsx are unverified, and the only thing that ever type-checks the demo is `tsc -b` inside docs.yml:46, meaning a demo type error surfaces as a failed gh-pages deploy rather than a failed PR. `apps/e2e` is excluded too, so the 16 Playwright tests never run anywhere. There is no `pnpm size` step, so the 12 kB budget in packages/core/package.json:76-79 is never enforced; no coverage step, so packages/core/vitest.config.ts:7-11's lcov reporter output is discarded; no `changeset status --since=origin/master` step, so PRs merge without a changeset (which is exactly why versions are hand-bumped and no CHANGELOG exists). `engines.node` is `>=18.0.0` (package.json:43) but only Node 22 is tested, and there is no `actions/cache` for `.turbo`, so every run is a cold cache.
findings.fix: In .github/workflows/ci.yml add `strategy.matrix.node: [18, 20, 22]` to the ci job; add an `actions/cache` step keyed on `${{ runner.os }}-turbo-${{ github.sha }}` with path `.turbo`; add `pnpm turbo run size`, `pnpm --filter @guideflow/core test -- --coverage`, and `pnpm changeset status --since=origin/master` steps; add a separate `e2e` job that runs `pnpm --filter e2e test` after `pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium`; and stop excluding `@guideflow/demo`/`storybook` from the type-check and lint steps.
findings.verifierNote: Verified every sub-claim independently: ci.yml lines 35/38/41/44 each carry the identical four `--filter=!` exclusions; the workflow has only build/type-check/lint/test — no size, coverage, changeset-status or actions/cache step; node-version is pinned to 22 alone (line 28) against engines `>=18.0.0` at root package.json:43; docs.yml:46 is `pnpm --filter @guideflow/demo build` whose script is `tsc -b && vite build`; packages/core/package.json:76-79 holds the 12 kB gzip budget and vitest.config.ts:7-11 the lcov reporter; .changeset/ contains only config.json. apps/demo/src/App.tsx is actually 926 lines, not ~400 — understated, which strengthens rather than weakens the point.

findings.title: Every clean script (and the root clean) uses POSIX `rm -rf`, which fails on the maintainer's Windows machine
findings.evidence: "clean": "turbo run clean && rm -rf node_modules",
findings.impact: `rm -rf` is not a cmd.exe builtin. `pnpm clean` on Windows fails at the root, and each of the eight per-package `clean` scripts fails identically: packages/core/package.json:63 (`rm -rf dist coverage .turbo`), packages/ai:56, packages/analytics:56, packages/react:55, packages/svelte:53, packages/vue:56, packages/cli:49, packages/devtools:12 (all `rm -rf dist .turbo`). Because turbo.json:34 marks `clean` as `cache: false`, every invocation re-runs and re-fails, so the documented recovery path in README.md:588 ("pnpm clean — Remove all build artifacts") does not work for the primary developer. The root script also only removes the root `node_modules`, leaving all nine `packages/*/node_modules` and `apps/*/node_modules` trees behind.
findings.fix: Add `rimraf` to root devDependencies and replace every `rm -rf X Y` with `rimraf X Y`. For the root script use `turbo run clean && rimraf node_modules "packages/*/node_modules" "apps/*/node_modules"` (rimraf handles the globs itself, cross-platform).
findings.verifierNote: Root package.json:14 is verbatim `"clean": "turbo run clean && rm -rf node_modules",`. I verified every per-package clean: core:63 `rm -rf dist coverage .turbo`, ai:56, analytics:56, react:55, svelte:54 (auditor said 53 — off by one), vue:56, cli:49, devtools:12 — all `rm -rf`. turbo.json:34 does mark clean `cache: false`. README.md:588 is `| \`pnpm clean\` | Remove all build artifacts |`. No shell-emulator in .npmrc. Severity lowered: this only breaks a convenience script on the maintainer's own platform — nothing published or CI-gated is affected.

findings.title: packages/cli has no test script at all — the whole CLI surface is untested and unverified
findings.evidence:
"scripts": {
    "build": "tsup",
    "dev": "tsup --watch",
    "lint": "eslint src --max-warnings 0",
    "type-check": "tsc --noEmit",
    "clean": "rm -rf dist .turbo"
  },
findings.impact: `turbo run test` skips packages/cli entirely. Nothing verifies the four commands, and two of them have logic that is very likely wrong: packages/cli/src/commands/export.ts:39 tries to extract a FlowDefinition with the regex `/\{[\s\S]*?id\s*:\s*['\"]([^'\"]+)['\"][\s\S]*?states\s*:\s*\{/` and, on a match, discards the flow and writes a stub `{ _note, rawSnippet }` (lines 47-50) — so `guideflow export` never actually exports a usable flow. packages/cli/src/index.ts:36-38 reads `../package.json` relative to `dist/`, which only works because the bin is one directory deep; a smoke test would pin that. There is also no test that the emitted bin is executable.
findings.fix: Add `vitest` to packages/cli devDependencies, a `"test": "vitest run"` script, and `packages/cli/src/__tests__/` covering: `export` round-tripping a real `.json` flow, `export` on a `.ts` flow (which should assert the current stub behaviour or be fixed), `init` writing the three template files into a tmpdir, and `push` against a mocked `fetch` for the 200/non-2xx/network-error branches.
findings.verifierNote: packages/cli/package.json:44-50 matches the quoted scripts block verbatim — build/dev/lint/type-check/clean, no test. The supporting defects also check out exactly: packages/cli/src/commands/export.ts:39 is the cited regex and lines 47-50 build `flowJson = { _note: 'Static extraction was used...', rawSnippet: match[0].slice(0, 500) }`, discarding the matched flow; packages/cli/src/index.ts:36-38 reads `resolve(__dirname, '..', 'package.json')`, which only works because the bin sits one level under the package root.

findings.title: packages/cli puts vite in `dependencies` for one command, forcing every CLI install to download Vite and its esbuild binary
findings.impact: README.md:528 tells users to `pnpm add -g @guideflow/cli`. Because vite is a hard dependency, that global install pulls Vite 5 plus rollup and a platform-specific esbuild binary — tens of megabytes — even for users who only ever run `guideflow init`, `export` or `push`. Vite is used by exactly one command, and packages/cli/src/commands/studio.ts:6 imports it statically at module top level (`import { createServer } from 'vite'`), so the cost is paid on every CLI startup, not just for `studio`.
findings.fix: Move `vite` from `dependencies` to `optionalDependencies` (or `peerDependenciesMeta.optional`) in packages/cli/package.json:56, and change packages/cli/src/commands/studio.ts:6 to a lazy `const { createServer } = await import('vite')` inside the `.action()` handler, wrapped so a missing module prints "guideflow studio requires vite — install it with `npm i -D vite`". `vite` is already in the tsup `external` list (packages/cli/tsup.config.ts:10), so the emitted bundle needs no change.
findings.verifierNote: packages/cli/package.json:56 is verbatim `"vite": "^5.2.0"` inside `dependencies` (lines 51-57), not devDependencies. packages/cli/src/commands/studio.ts:6 is `import { createServer } from 'vite';` at module top level, and packages/cli/src/index.ts:31 imports studioCommand unconditionally, so vite is loaded on every CLI invocation including `init`, `export` and `push`. README.md:528 does instruct `pnpm add -g @guideflow/cli`.

findings.title: @guideflow/core build uses POSIX `cp -r`; on Windows the ./styles export subpath is never produced
findings.evidence: "build": "tsup && cp -r src/styles dist/styles",
findings.impact: pnpm runs lifecycle scripts through cmd.exe on Windows. On a clean Windows checkout without Git's Unix tools on PATH, `pnpm --filter @guideflow/core build` prints "'cp' is not recognized as an internal or external command" and exits non-zero, so `dist/styles/` is never created. Every downstream consumer of `import '@guideflow/core/styles'` (packages/core/package.json:41, README.md:87, apps/storybook/.storybook/preview.ts:2, packages/cli/src/commands/init.ts:9 scaffolding) then fails to resolve, and `turbo run build` aborts the whole graph because core is the root dependency of every other package. CI is ubuntu-latest so this is invisible to CI and only breaks the maintainer's own machine and any Windows contributor.
findings.fix: Add `cpy-cli` (or a tiny `scripts/copy-styles.mjs` using `node:fs` `cpSync(src, dest, { recursive: true })`) to packages/core devDependencies and change the script to `tsup && node ../../scripts/copy-styles.mjs` or `tsup && cpy "src/styles/**/*.css" dist/styles`. A `node:fs` script is preferable — it adds no dependency and matches the existing pattern already used in packages/devtools/vite.config.ts:4.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/package.json:57 is verbatim `"build": "tsup && cp -r src/styles dist/styles",`. .npmrc contains only `access=public` — no `shell-emulator=true`, so pnpm 8 uses cmd.exe on Windows and `cp` is not a builtin. dist/styles/ is required by the ./styles subpath (line 41-46) and is imported by apps/storybook/.storybook/preview.ts:2, README, and packages/cli/src/commands/init.ts:9. Severity lowered: CI is ubuntu-latest and the npm tarball is built there, so nothing published is broken — this is a maintainer/contributor DX break, not a shipped-broken P0.

findings.title: core builds an IIFE bundle for CDN use but declares no unpkg/jsdelivr/browser field, so script-tag users get the CJS file
findings.evidence:
format: ['esm', 'cjs', 'iife'],
  globalName: 'GuideFlow',
findings.impact: The IIFE target produces `dist/index.global.js` (67,839 bytes, confirmed present) with a `GuideFlow` global, and packages/core/src/index.ts:344-352 documents `getGuideFlow()` as the "Default singleton — for script-tag / CDN usage". But packages/core/package.json declares no `unpkg`, `jsdelivr` or `browser` field and no `./global` export subpath, so unpkg and jsDelivr fall back to `main` (line 48) = `./dist/index.cjs`. A `<script src="https://unpkg.com/@guideflow/core">` therefore loads a CommonJS module and dies on `module.exports`/`require` being undefined. The IIFE build is dead weight in every tarball, and there is no documentation anywhere of the `GuideFlow.*` global.
findings.fix: Add `"unpkg": "./dist/index.global.js"`, `"jsdelivr": "./dist/index.global.js"` and an `"./global": "./dist/index.global.js"` export subpath to packages/core/package.json, then document the script-tag usage (`<script src="…/index.global.js"></script>` + `GuideFlow.createGuideFlow()`) in README.md. If CDN support is not actually intended, drop `'iife'` and `globalName` from packages/core/tsup.config.ts:5-6 instead.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/tsup.config.ts:5-6 is verbatim `format: ['esm', 'cjs', 'iife'],` / `globalName: 'GuideFlow',`. dist/index.global.js exists at exactly 67,839 bytes. packages/core/package.json has no unpkg, jsdelivr or browser field and no ./global export subpath — I read the full manifest — so `main` (line 48) `./dist/index.cjs` is what unpkg/jsDelivr serve. packages/core/src/index.ts:344-352 does carry the "Default singleton — for script-tag / CDN usage" comment above getGuideFlow(), confirming the intent that the IIFE build was meant to satisfy.

findings.title: The "./styles" and "./styles/*" export subpaths declare only an `import` condition, so non-ESM resolvers get ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED
findings.impact: A conditional exports object with no `default` key fails to resolve for any consumer whose condition set does not include `import`. That covers Jest's default `require`-based moduleNameMapper, `next/jest`, PostCSS/`css-loader` resolution chains that use the `style` condition, Sass `@use`, and plain `require('@guideflow/core/styles')` — all get `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED: No "exports" main defined`. Users importing the stylesheet from a test setup file or a CJS build step cannot load it at all, and there is no `"style"` condition for CSS-aware bundlers to prefer.
findings.fix: In packages/core/package.json:41-46 give both subpaths a terminal fallback and a style condition: `"./styles": { "style": "./dist/styles/index.css", "default": "./dist/styles/index.css" }` and `"./styles/*": { "style": "./dist/styles/*", "default": "./dist/styles/*" }`. Also add `"./styles/*.css": "./dist/styles/*.css"` so explicit-extension imports resolve.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/package.json:41-46 quoted verbatim — both `./styles` and `./styles/*` have only an `import` key and no `default`/`require`/`style`. Node throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED for any resolver whose condition set lacks `import`. Severity lowered: the two highest-traffic paths (Vite and webpack resolving a CSS import from an ESM module) do include the `import` condition and work today; the breakage is confined to CJS require, Sass/PostCSS chains, and some Jest setups, and most Jest configs stub CSS via moduleNameMapper before resolution.

findings.title: apps/demo ships an .eslintrc.json but no lint script, and CI excludes it from type-check — its only gate is the docs deploy
findings.impact: apps/demo/.eslintrc.json exists and carefully disables six rules (lines 4-9), which only makes sense if the app is meant to be linted — but there is no `lint` script, so `turbo run lint` skips it and that config is dead. Separately, ci.yml:38 excludes `@guideflow/demo` from `type-check`, so the ~400-line apps/demo/src/App.tsx is not type-checked on PRs; the only place it is checked is `tsc -b` inside `pnpm --filter @guideflow/demo build` at .github/workflows/docs.yml:46, which runs post-merge. A type error in the demo therefore passes CI, merges, and then breaks the gh-pages deployment. Note also that `tsc -b` emits into apps/demo/dist (tsconfig.json:7 `"outDir": "dist"`, `composite: true`) and the subsequent `vite build` empties that same directory, so the tsc output is written and immediately discarded.
findings.fix: Add `"lint": "eslint src --max-warnings 0"` to apps/demo/package.json:6-11, stop excluding `@guideflow/demo` from the type-check and lint steps in .github/workflows/ci.yml:38 and :41, and change the build script to `"build": "tsc --noEmit && vite build"` so type-checking does not emit throwaway output.
findings.verifierNote: apps/demo/package.json:6-11 matches verbatim — dev/build/preview/type-check, no lint. apps/demo/.eslintrc.json exists and disables exactly six rules at lines 4-9, dead config with no script to load it. ci.yml:38 does exclude @guideflow/demo from type-check, and docs.yml:46 (`pnpm --filter @guideflow/demo build` → `tsc -b && vite build`) is the only place it is checked, post-merge. The tsc-output claim also holds: apps/demo/tsconfig.json:7 sets `"outDir": "dist"` with composite:true and no noEmit, and vite's emptyOutDir defaults to true for an outDir inside root, so the emitted JS is wiped immediately.

findings.title: Every dual-format package emits dist/index.d.cts but no `exports` map references it, so CJS consumers get ESM-flavoured types
findings.impact: tsup with `format: ['esm','cjs']` and `dts: true` emits BOTH `dist/index.d.ts` and `dist/index.d.cts` — I confirmed both files exist in packages/{core,ai,analytics,react,svelte,vue}/dist. Because the package is `"type": "module"` and a single top-level `"types"` key is hoisted above the conditions, TypeScript under `moduleResolution: node16/nodenext/bundler` resolves the `require` branch to `dist/index.cjs` (CJS) but its types to `dist/index.d.ts`, which TS treats as an ES module. This is the classic "Masquerading as ESM / FalseESM" failure: a consumer doing `const { createGuideFlow } = require('@guideflow/core')` in a CJS TS project gets `TS2497`/`esModuleInterop` errors or a namespace-shaped type with no callable members, and `createGuideFlow` appears to not exist. Affects all six published libraries identically.
findings.fix: Replace the flat condition object in packages/{core,ai,analytics,react,svelte,vue}/package.json with nested per-condition types: `".": { "import": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" }, "require": { "types": "./dist/index.d.cts", "default": "./dist/index.cjs" } }`. Keep the legacy top-level `main`/`module`/`types` for node10 resolvers but point `types` at `./dist/index.d.cts` since `main` is the CJS file.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/package.json:35-40 quoted verbatim. I confirmed dist/index.d.cts exists alongside dist/index.d.ts in all six dual-format packages (core, ai, analytics, react, svelte, vue — 23,522 bytes each for core, identical size). tsup config has format ['esm','cjs'] + dts:true and no exports entry references .d.cts, so a require-condition consumer under node16/nodenext gets a .d.ts inside a "type":"module" package — the FalseESM/Masquerading-as-ESM case. Severity lowered: this is a types-only defect under specific moduleResolution modes; runtime require() works, and `bundler` resolution (what most consumers use) is unaffected.

findings.title: No CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, .nvmrc, .editorconfig, issue/PR templates, CHANGELOG or npm provenance
findings.evidence: name: CI
findings.impact: `git ls-files` shows the root contains only .eslintrc.json, .gitignore, .npmrc, .prettierrc.json, LICENSE, README.md, package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, pnpm-workspace.yaml, repo.config.json, tsconfig.base.json, turbo.json, and `.github` contains only the three workflow files. So: no SECURITY.md (there is no channel to report a vulnerability in a library that injects DOM and forwards analytics to third parties), no CONTRIBUTING.md or CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md (README.md:558-603 carries an abbreviated contributing section instead), no issue or PR templates, no dependabot.yml, no .nvmrc despite CI pinning Node 22, no .editorconfig, and no CHANGELOG.md in any package even though versions have been bumped nine times — .changeset/ contains only config.json, confirming no changeset has ever been written. None of the seven publishable manifests sets `publishConfig.provenance: true`, so the npm packages carry no attestation linking them to this repo even though release.yml already runs in GitHub Actions where provenance is free.
findings.fix: Add SECURITY.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, .nvmrc (`22`), .editorconfig, .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/{bug_report.yml,feature_request.yml}, .github/pull_request_template.md and .github/dependabot.yml. Add `"provenance": true` to the existing `publishConfig` block in each of the seven publishable manifests (e.g. packages/core/package.json:32) and `id-token: write` to the release job permissions in .github/workflows/release.yml:16-18. Start writing changesets so CHANGELOG.md files are generated.
findings.verifierNote: `git ls-files` at the root returns exactly .eslintrc.json, .gitignore, .npmrc, .prettierrc.json, LICENSE, README.md, package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, pnpm-workspace.yaml, repo.config.json, tsconfig.base.json, turbo.json — and `git ls-files .github` returns only the three workflow files. So no SECURITY.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, issue/PR templates, dependabot.yml, .nvmrc or .editorconfig. .changeset/ contains only config.json. I read all seven publishable manifests and none sets publishConfig.provenance — each has only `"access": "public"`. The cited file/line (ci.yml:1 `name: CI`) is a placeholder anchor rather than real evidence, but every enumerated absence is independently verified.

findings.title: No package ships a LICENSE file — `files` omits it and no per-package LICENSE exists
findings.evidence:
"files": [
    "dist",
    "src",
    "README.md"
  ],
findings.impact: npm auto-includes a LICENSE file only from the package's own root directory, and I confirmed none of packages/{core,react,vue,svelte,ai,analytics,cli} contains a LICENSE file — the only one is the repo-root LICENSE, which is outside every package tarball. So all six published packages declare `"license": "MIT"` but ship no license text, which fails corporate license-scanning tools (FOSSA, Snyk license policies, `license-checker`) and leaves downstream redistributors without the attribution notice the MIT license itself requires. The identical `files` array appears in all seven publishable manifests (packages/react:44, vue:44, svelte:44, ai:45, analytics:45, cli:39).
findings.fix: Add `"LICENSE"` to the `files` array in all seven manifests and copy the root LICENSE into each package directory — either by committing seven copies, or (cleaner) by adding a `prepack` script `node scripts/copy-license.mjs` that `cpSync`s the root LICENSE into the package before packing.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/package.json:51-55 is verbatim `"files": ["dist", "src", "README.md"]`. A recursive search for LICENSE* under packages/ (excluding node_modules) returned nothing — the only LICENSE is at the repo root, outside every package directory, so npm's automatic root-LICENSE inclusion has nothing to include. The identical files array appears in react:44, vue:44, svelte:44, ai:45, analytics:45 and cli:39, and all seven declare `"license": "MIT"`.

findings.title: `pnpm test:e2e` is a silent no-op — apps/e2e defines `test`, not `test:e2e`
findings.evidence: "test:e2e": "turbo run test:e2e",
findings.impact: turbo.json:18 defines a `test:e2e` task, but no package in the workspace has a `test:e2e` script — apps/e2e/package.json:5-9 defines `test`, `test:ui` and `test:headed`. `turbo run test:e2e` therefore matches zero packages and exits 0, so README.md:581 ("pnpm test:e2e — Run Playwright end-to-end tests") is false. Worse, because apps/e2e names its Playwright script `test`, the root `pnpm test` (package.json:9, `turbo run test`) *does* pick it up and will try to launch browsers during what users expect to be a unit-test run.
findings.fix: Rename apps/e2e/package.json:6 from `"test"` to `"test:e2e": "playwright test"` (and `test:ui`/`test:headed` to `test:e2e:ui`/`test:e2e:headed`). That makes the root `test:e2e` script work and stops `pnpm test` from booting a browser.
findings.verifierNote: Root package.json:10 is verbatim `"test:e2e": "turbo run test:e2e",` and turbo.json:18 defines the task, but I grepped every workspace manifest and no package declares a `test:e2e` script — apps/e2e/package.json:5-9 has test/test:ui/test:headed. README.md:581 documents it as working. The inverse is also true: apps/e2e's script is named `test`, so root `pnpm test` (package.json:9) does match it and turbo will launch Playwright during what reads as a unit-test run.

findings.title: The 12 kB core size budget is never run in CI, and the actual unminified shipped file gzips to 14.9 kB
findings.impact: README.md:40 advertises core at "~12 kB gzip" and README.md:7 renders a bundlephobia minzip badge. But packages/core/tsup.config.ts:12 sets `minify: false`, so the file actually published is unminified: `dist/index.js` is 63,663 bytes raw and gzips to 14,879 bytes (14.5 kB) — which is what bundlephobia and any CDN consumer measures. size-limit's own number will be lower because @size-limit/preset-small-lib re-bundles with esbuild minification before measuring, so the configured gate does not measure the artifact users download. And it is moot either way: no workflow runs `turbo run size` (ci.yml has build/type-check/lint/test only), so the budget has never been checked. `pnpm size` (package.json:13) also only ever covers core — no other package declares a `size` script or a `size-limit` block.
findings.fix: Add a `pnpm turbo run size` step to .github/workflows/ci.yml, and make the budget measure reality: either set `minify: true` in packages/core/tsup.config.ts:12, or add a second size-limit entry with `"gzip": true` and no bundler (`"path": "./dist/index.js", "limit": "15 kB"`) so the published-file size is gated. Then reconcile the number quoted in README.md:40.
findings.verifierNote: packages/core/package.json:75-81 is verbatim. I reproduced the measurement myself: dist/index.js is 63,663 bytes raw and 14,899 bytes gzipped (auditor said 14,879 — level-dependent, same conclusion), against a 12 kB budget and README.md:40's "~12 kB gzip" claim plus the bundlephobia minzip badge at README.md:7. packages/core/tsup.config.ts:12 is `minify: false`, confirming the published file is unminified. ci.yml has only build/type-check/lint/test — no `turbo run size` anywhere in any workflow — and core is the only package with a `size` script or size-limit block.

findings.title: Root `pnpm studio` fails — the `guideflow` bin is not linked into any node_modules/.bin
findings.evidence: "studio": "pnpm --filter @guideflow/cli exec guideflow studio",
findings.impact: pnpm links the bins of a package's *dependencies*, never a package's own bin into its own `node_modules/.bin`. I confirmed this: `node_modules/.bin` contains changeset, eslint, playwright, prettier, size-limit, tsc, turbo, vitest — no `guideflow`; and `packages/cli/node_modules/.bin` contains only tsc, tsserver, tsup, vite. So `pnpm studio` exits with "Command failed: guideflow" / command-not-found. The script also has no build dependency, so even with a linked bin it would fail on a fresh clone because `packages/cli/dist/index.js` (the bin target, packages/cli/package.json:32) does not exist yet.
findings.fix: Change package.json:22 to `"studio": "pnpm --filter @guideflow/cli run build && node packages/cli/dist/index.js studio"`, or add `"guideflow": "workspace:*"`-style self-reference by listing `@guideflow/cli` in the root devDependencies so pnpm links its bin at the root.
findings.verifierNote: Root package.json:22 is verbatim. I listed node_modules/.bin: changeset, eslint, playwright, prettier, size-limit, tsc, tsserver, turbo, vitest (+ .CMD/.ps1) — no guideflow. packages/cli/node_modules/.bin holds only tsc, tsserver, tsup, tsup-node, vite. pnpm links dependencies' bins, and no manifest depends on @guideflow/cli, so its own bin (packages/cli/package.json:31-33) is never linked. The script also has no build prerequisite, so dist/index.js would be missing on a fresh clone.

findings.title: @guideflow/svelte's CJS build calls require('svelte/store'), which throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM — the advertised `require` entry point is dead
findings.evidence: require('svelte/store')
findings.impact: I verified svelte@4.2.20's own package.json declares `"type": "module"` and its `./store` subpath exports only `{ "types": "./types/index.d.ts", "default": "./src/runtime/store/index.js" }` — an ES module with no `require` condition. So `require('@guideflow/svelte')`, which packages/svelte/package.json:39 and :42 both advertise (`"require": "./dist/index.cjs"`, `"main": "./dist/index.cjs"`), crashes at load time with `Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module .../svelte/src/runtime/store/index.js`. Svelte 5, also in the peer range `^4.0.0 || ^5.0.0` (packages/svelte/package.json:60), is ESM-only and fails the same way. Any SvelteKit SSR path, Jest/CJS test runner, or `tsc`-emitted CommonJS build that pulls in the adapter breaks.
findings.fix: Drop `cjs` from `format` in packages/svelte/tsup.config.ts:5 (make it `format: ['esm']`), remove `"require": "./dist/index.cjs"` and `"main": "./dist/index.cjs"` from packages/svelte/package.json:39/:42, and keep only `"module"`/`"exports".".".import`. Svelte's own ecosystem is ESM-only, so an ESM-only adapter is correct.
findings.verifierNote: The evidence line is wrong — dist/index.cjs:1 is `'use strict';`; `var store = require('svelte/store');` is on line 4. The underlying fact holds: node_modules/.pnpm/svelte@4.2.20 declares `"type": "module"` and `"./store": { "types": "./types/index.d.ts", "default": "./src/runtime/store/index.js" }` with no require condition. But the stated impact is overstated: SvelteKit SSR is ESM and resolves the `import` condition, never dist/index.cjs; and Node 20.19+/22.12+ support require(ESM) unflagged, so the ERR_REQUIRE_ESM window is Node 18–20.18 plus CJS test runners only.

findings.title: turbo.json's globalDependencies omit tsconfig.base.json, .eslintrc.json and pnpm-lock.yaml, so shared-config edits return stale cached successes
findings.evidence: "globalDependencies": ["**/.env.*local"],
findings.impact: Turbo hashes only each package's own files plus the listed global dependencies. Because tsconfig.base.json is not listed, tightening or relaxing any of the eight strict flags there (`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, `isolatedModules`, `target`, `lib`, `moduleResolution`) leaves every `build` and `type-check` task hash unchanged, so `turbo run type-check` replays a cached PASS without ever invoking tsc. The same holds for .eslintrc.json versus `lint` and for pnpm-lock.yaml versus everything. A maintainer can turn on a strict flag, watch CI go green, and ship code that does not type-check.
findings.fix: Change turbo.json:3 to `"globalDependencies": ["**/.env.*local", "tsconfig.base.json", ".eslintrc.json", ".prettierrc.json", "pnpm-lock.yaml", "package.json"]`.
findings.verifierNote: turbo.json:3 is verbatim `"globalDependencies": ["**/.env.*local"],` and tsconfig.base.json / .eslintrc.json are root-level files owned by no package, so they genuinely are outside every task hash — the strict-flag scenario (tsconfig.base.json:8-19 lists exactly the eight flags cited) is real. The pnpm-lock.yaml half is refuted: Turborepo 1.x automatically hashes the workspace lockfile for external-dependency change detection; it does not need to be listed in globalDependencies.

findings.title: turbo's `lint` task has no dependsOn, so `pnpm lint` on a fresh clone fails — type-aware ESLint needs dependency .d.ts files
findings.impact: .eslintrc.json:8 extends `plugin:@typescript-eslint/recommended-requiring-type-checking` with `parserOptions.project: true` (.eslintrc.json:12-14), so ESLint builds a full TS program for every linted file. `packages/react/src/index.ts:43` imports types from `@guideflow/core`, which resolves through packages/core/package.json:50 `"types": "./dist/index.d.ts"`. On a clean checkout that file does not exist, so the program has `any` everywhere and the `no-unsafe-assignment` / `no-unsafe-member-access` / `no-unsafe-call` rules fire en masse, plus `import/no-unresolved`. `pnpm lint` therefore fails for every adapter package unless the user happens to run `pnpm build` first. CI only survives because ci.yml:35 runs build before ci.yml:41 runs lint.
findings.fix: Add `"dependsOn": ["^build"]` to the `lint` task in turbo.json:23-25, matching what `test` (line 14) and `type-check` (line 27) already declare.
findings.verifierNote: turbo.json:23-25 is verbatim `"lint": { "outputs": [] }` with no dependsOn, while build/test/test:e2e/type-check all declare `dependsOn: ["^build"]`. .eslintrc.json:8 extends recommended-requiring-type-checking and :12-14 sets `parserOptions.project: true`. I checked packages/react/tsconfig.json — no path mapping to core's src, so `@guideflow/core` resolves via packages/core/package.json:50 `"types": "./dist/index.d.ts"`. packages/react/src/context.tsx:5 imports the *value* `createGuideFlow` and calls it, so with dist absent it is `any` and no-unsafe-call/no-unsafe-assignment fire under `--max-warnings 0`. ci.yml:35 runs build before ci.yml:41 lint, which is exactly why CI survives.

findings.title: packages/vue ships a test script, vitest and @vue/test-utils but has no tests and no vitest config — a fabricated green test run
findings.evidence: "test": "vitest run --passWithNoTests",
findings.impact: There is no `packages/vue/src/__tests__` directory and no `packages/vue/vitest.config.ts` (the only vitest configs are in ai, analytics, core, react). `--passWithNoTests` converts vitest's "No test files found" error into exit 0, so `turbo run test` reports `@guideflow/vue:test` as passing while executing nothing. `packages/vue/src/plugin.ts` and `packages/vue/src/composables/use-tour.ts` — the entire public surface exported at packages/vue/src/index.ts:19-24 — are completely untested. `@vue/test-utils` (line 66) and `vitest` (line 69) are installed purely as decoration; `@vitejs/plugin-vue` (line 65) is also unused since tsup never processes .vue files. The same `--passWithNoTests` masking applies to packages/ai/package.json:53 and packages/react/package.json:52, though those two do have real tests.
findings.fix: Either write the tests — add packages/vue/vitest.config.ts (environment `happy-dom`, mirroring packages/react/vitest.config.ts) plus `packages/vue/src/__tests__/use-tour.test.ts` and `plugin.test.ts` — and drop `--passWithNoTests`; or, if Vue coverage is deferred, remove the `test` script, `vitest`, `@vue/test-utils` and `@vitejs/plugin-vue` so the gap is visible instead of hidden.
findings.verifierNote: packages/vue/package.json:53 is verbatim `"test": "vitest run --passWithNoTests",`. I enumerated all vitest configs — ai, analytics, core, react only — and all __tests__ directories — ai, analytics, core, react only. packages/vue/src contains exactly index.ts, plugin.ts and composables/use-tour.ts, which is the whole surface exported at index.ts:19-24. @vue/test-utils (line 66), vitest (line 69) and @vitejs/plugin-vue (line 65) are unused — there is no vite/vitest config in the package for the plugin to be loaded by.

findings.title: `clean` script uses `rm -rf`, which fails on Windows PowerShell/cmd
findings.evidence: "clean": "rm -rf dist .turbo"
findings.impact: `pnpm --filter @guideflow/cli clean` (and root `turbo run clean`) fails with `rm : The term 'rm' is not recognized` on a stock Windows shell. This monorepo is developed on Windows (the working tree is `C:\Users\InnFuture\Work\GuideFlow`), so the maintainer's own clean step is broken outside Git Bash. The same pattern is in packages/core/package.json:63, and packages/core/package.json:57 uses `cp -r src/styles dist/styles` in `build` — meaning `@guideflow/core/styles`, which the CLI's own scaffolded `guideflow.ts` imports (init.ts:9), cannot be produced by a Windows-native build at all.
findings.fix: Replace with `rimraf dist .turbo` (add `rimraf` as a devDependency) or Node's `node -e "fs.rmSync('dist',{recursive:true,force:true})"`. For core's build, swap `cp -r` for `cpy-cli`/`shx cp -r`, or emit the CSS through tsup so no shell copy is needed.
findings.verifierNote: packages/cli/package.json:49 `"clean": "rm -rf dist .turbo"` verbatim. packages/core/package.json:63 is `"clean": "rm -rf dist coverage .turbo"` and :57 is `"build": "tsup && cp -r src/styles dist/styles"` — both line numbers confirmed by reading the file. I checked for the obvious escape: .npmrc contains only `access=public`, so pnpm's shell-emulator is off and lifecycle scripts run through cmd.exe on Windows, where rm and cp do not exist. The working tree is C:\Users\InnFuture\Work\GuideFlow, so the maintainer is affected. init.ts:9 does emit `import '@guideflow/core/styles'`, making the cp -r in core's build load-bearing.

findings.title: `init` hardcodes `pnpm add` and never installs or records dependencies
findings.evidence:
const pkgName = framework === 'none' ? 'core' : framework;
    console.log(`    ${chalk.cyan(`pnpm add @guideflow/core @guideflow/${pkgName}`)}`);
findings.impact: No detection of `npm_config_user_agent`, no lockfile probing (`package-lock.json` / `yarn.lock` / `pnpm-lock.yaml` / `bun.lockb`), so every npm and yarn user is told to run a pnpm command. It also never touches the target `package.json`, so the files it just wrote (`import { createGuideFlow } from '@guideflow/core'`, `import '@guideflow/core/styles'`) will not compile until the user manually runs the printed command. For `framework === 'none'` the printed line is `pnpm add @guideflow/core @guideflow/core` — the package listed twice.
findings.fix: Detect the manager from `process.env.npm_config_user_agent` (falling back to lockfile presence) and print the matching `npm install` / `yarn add` / `pnpm add` / `bun add`. Deduplicate the package list when `framework === 'none'`. Offer an `--install` flag that shells out to the detected manager.
findings.verifierNote: init.ts:111-112 verbatim. No npm_config_user_agent read and no lockfile probe anywhere in the package; the target package.json is never modified (the only fs writes are the three writeFileSync calls at 95-99 and mkdirSync at 92), so the emitted `import { createGuideFlow } from '@guideflow/core'` cannot resolve until the user acts. For framework 'none', pkgName is 'core', producing the duplicated `pnpm add @guideflow/core @guideflow/core`. Downgrading: the output is advisory console text, not a broken artifact — no data loss, no failed command, trivially fixed by the user. That is a notable DX gap (P2), not a serious defect.

findings.title: `init` always emits TypeScript and has no JS mode, so it produces uncompilable files in a JavaScript project
findings.evidence:
const FLOW_TEMPLATE = `import { gf } from './guideflow';
import type { FlowDefinition } from '@guideflow/core';
findings.impact: `my-tour.ts` uses `import type` and the annotation `const welcomeTour: FlowDefinition = {` (line 30); `GuideFlowProvider.tsx` uses `{ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }` (line 20). File extensions are hardcoded `.ts`/`.tsx` at lines 95-99 with no `--typescript`/`--js` flag and no probe for `tsconfig.json`. Dropped into a plain JS/Vite or CRA JavaScript project, these files fail to parse. Additionally, both `FLOW_TEMPLATE` and `REACT_TEMPLATE` use the extensionless relative specifier `'./guideflow'`, which is invalid under Node16/NodeNext ESM resolution — the CLI's own tsconfig (packages/cli/tsconfig.json:6-7) uses exactly that setting, so the emitted code would not typecheck under the project's own conventions.
findings.fix: Detect TypeScript (presence of `tsconfig.json`, or a `--typescript`/`--js` flag), and add JS variants of the three templates with the type annotations stripped and `.js`/`.jsx` extensions. Emit `'./guideflow.js'` in the generated imports so the output is valid under NodeNext resolution as well as bundler resolution.
findings.verifierNote: The core claim checks out: FLOW_TEMPLATE at init.ts:25-26 is verbatim, `const welcomeTour: FlowDefinition = {` is at line 30, REACT_TEMPLATE:20 has `{ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }`, extensions are hardcoded .ts/.tsx at 95-99, and there is no --typescript/--js flag or tsconfig probe. But the NodeNext sub-claim is a stretch: packages/cli/tsconfig.json:6-7 does set module/moduleResolution NodeNext, yet that tsconfig governs the CLI's own sources, not files emitted into a stranger's project — those are consumed by the user's bundler (Vite/CRA/Next), where extensionless './guideflow' is standard and resolves fine. Downgrading to P2: TS-only scaffolding is a defensible default (docs at apps/docs/api/cli.md:30 do offer 'Vanilla' as a framework, not as a language), making this a notable gap rather than a serious defect.

findings.title: Neither export nor push validates that the JSON is a FlowDefinition before writing or publishing it
findings.impact: The only structural expectation is an optional `id`, used purely for the spinner label (`flow.id ?? 'unknown'`, line 50). `FlowDefinition` requires `id`, `initial`, and `states` (packages/core/src/types/index.ts:104-109), none of which is checked, and `body` — the raw file text, not the parsed object — is what gets POSTed (line 60). So `guideflow push package.json` happily uploads an unrelated file, and the `export` stub `{_note, rawSnippet}` from export.ts:47 sails through as `Pushing flow unknown…`. `export.ts:33-35` is equally unchecked on the `.json` path. There is also no `--dry-run` to inspect what would be sent, and `--env` (push.ts:26) documents `production | staging | preview` but accepts any string and forwards it verbatim in the `X-GuideFlow-Env` header (line 58).
findings.fix: Add a shared `validateFlow(obj): string[]` helper in the CLI asserting `id: string`, `initial: string`, `states: object`, `initial in states`, and each state's `steps[].id`; call it in export before writing and in push before POSTing, printing every problem and exiting non-zero. Add `--dry-run` to push that prints the resolved endpoint, headers (key redacted) and payload size. Constrain `--env` with Commander's `.choices(['production','staging','preview'])`.
findings.verifierNote: push.ts:42-48 verbatim; the parsed object is typed `{ id?: string }` and used only at line 50 for the spinner label, while line 60 posts `body` — the raw file text read at line 41 — so nothing structural is ever checked. FlowDefinition at packages/core/src/types/index.ts:104-108 requires id, initial and states (verified verbatim), none of which is validated. export.ts:33-35 likewise only JSON.parse's the .json path. --env at push.ts:26 documents 'production | staging | preview' but is a free-form string forwarded verbatim in the X-GuideFlow-Env header at line 58, as claimed. No --dry-run exists on either command.

findings.title: Vite is a hard runtime dependency of every command because studio.ts is statically imported
findings.evidence: import { studioCommand } from './commands/studio.js';
findings.impact: `studio.ts:6` does `import { createServer } from 'vite'` at module scope, and tsup marks `vite` external (tsup.config.ts:10), so `vite` (packages/cli/package.json:56, `"vite": "^5.2.0"`) is installed and loaded for `npx @guideflow/cli init`, `export`, and `push` alike. That is tens of megabytes and hundreds of transitive packages downloaded to run a command that writes two text files, and it materially slows CLI startup for every invocation. It also means the CLI drags its own Vite 5 into projects on Vite 6/7 — and since `createServer({root})` auto-loads the user's `vite.config.ts`, a config written against a newer Vite API will be evaluated by the CLI's older Vite and can fail.
findings.fix: Make the vite import lazy: move `const { createServer } = await import('vite')` inside the studio action handler, and move `vite` to `peerDependencies` + `peerDependenciesMeta.vite.optional = true` (or `optionalDependencies`), with a clear "install vite to use `guideflow studio`" error when the dynamic import fails. Widen the range to `^5 || ^6 || ^7` so it can reuse the project's own Vite.
findings.verifierNote: index.ts:31 verbatim; studio.ts:6 `import { createServer } from 'vite'` is a top-level ESM import, tsup.config.ts:10 lists 'vite' as external, and package.json:56 has `"vite": "^5.2.0"` under dependencies (not devDependencies). Since tsup bundles src into one ESM entry with vite external, the vite import is evaluated on every invocation including init/export/push. The vite.config.ts claim is also correct — createServer({root}) auto-resolves the user's config by default, so a Vite 6/7 config would be loaded by the CLI's Vite 5. 'Materially slows startup' is the one unmeasured assertion, but the eager-load and install-weight facts stand.

findings.title: The Intro.js migration guide's flow shape crashes and its event/method mapping does not exist
findings.evidence:
gf.start({
  id: 'hello-world',
  steps: [
    { id: '1', body: 'Hello World! 👋', target: '#step1', placement: 'bottom' },
findings.impact: `FlowDefinition` requires `initial` and `states` (types/index.ts:104-109); there is no top-level `steps`, and `Step` requires `content`, not `body`. Running the documented snippet reaches `new FlowMachine(flow)` → `if (!(flow.initial in flow.states))` with `flow.states === undefined`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot use 'in' operator to search for 'undefined' in undefined` (machine.ts:16) — the copy-paste migration path crashes immediately. The concept table is also wrong on three rows: `gf.end()` is not on `GuideFlowInstance` (only `stop()` is declared; it works at runtime purely because the instance is the TourEngine, so TS users get a compile error), and `'tour:end'` / `'tour:skip'` are not members of `TourEvents` (the real names are `tour:complete` and `step:skip`), so those `gf.on(...)` calls fail to type-check and never fire.
findings.fix: Rewrite the "After (GuideFlow — programmatic)" example with `initial`/`states`/`content`, and correct the mapping rows to `gf.stop()`, `gf.on('tour:complete')`, `gf.on('tour:abandon')`. Either add `end()` to the `GuideFlowInstance` interface as a documented alias of `stop()` or stop referencing it.
findings.verifierNote: Verified the snippet in apps/docs/guide/migrate-intro.md (gf.start({ id, steps: [{ id, body, target, placement }] }) — the cited line 52 is one line off from the `gf.start({` opener at 51, but the quoted content is present). FlowDefinition requires initial+states (types/index.ts:104-109) and Step requires `content` (line 57), so the call reaches `new FlowMachine(flow)` via index.ts:262 → tour.ts:100 and hits `if (!(flow.initial in flow.states))` at machine.ts:16 with states undefined → TypeError. Concept table verified verbatim: line 15 maps `.exit()` to `gf.end()` (GuideFlowInstance declares only stop(), index.ts:99), line 19 uses 'tour:end' and line 20 'tour:skip', neither of which exists in TourEvents (types/index.ts:202-216).

findings.title: Docs claim start() throws when a tour is active; it silently abandons the running tour
findings.evidence: | `start(flow)` | Begin a tour. Throws if a tour is already active. |
findings.impact: `TourEngine.start` begins with `if (this._active) this._doEnd(false)` (tour.ts:97) — it emits `tour:abandon` for the previous flow and continues. Callers that (per the docs) wrap `start()` in try/catch to detect an already-running tour will never see an exception, and analytics consumers get a surprise `tour:abandon` for a flow the user never dismissed. apps/docs/api/create-guide-flow.md:64 additionally documents an `ai` property on the instance ("| `ai` | AI module (if `@guideflow/ai` is configured) |") that exists nowhere in `GuideFlowInstance` or the `Object.assign` literal.
findings.fix: Either implement the documented behaviour (throw, or return early with a warning, when `_active`) or fix the doc to "Starts a tour; if one is already running it is abandoned first (emits `tour:abandon`)". Remove the `ai` row from create-guide-flow.md or add the property.
findings.verifierNote: apps/docs/api/tour-engine.md:41 is verbatim '| `start(flow)` | Begin a tour. Throws if a tour is already active. |'. TourEngine.start begins `if (this._active) this._doEnd(false)` (tour.ts:97), and _doEnd(false) emits tour:abandon (tour.ts:311) — no throw exists on that path. Also verified apps/docs/api/create-guide-flow.md:64 '| `ai` | AI module (if `@guideflow/ai` is configured) |'; GuideFlowInstance (index.ts:89-141) and the Object.assign literal (214-318) contain no `ai` member.

findings.title: FlowMachine.send() transitions into a non-existent target state, leaving an active but invisible tour
findings.evidence:
this._callExit(this._ctx.currentState)
    this._ctx.history.push(target)
    this._ctx.currentState = target
    this._ctx.stepIndex = 0
    this._callEntry(target)
findings.impact: The constructor validates `flow.initial` (machine.ts:16-20) and `restore()` validates its snapshot state (line 140), but `send()` never checks `target in this._ctx.flow.states`. A typo (`on: { NEXT: 'featurs' }`) transitions successfully — `send` returns `true` — into a state that does not exist: `currentSteps` becomes `[]`, `currentStep` is `null`, `isFinal` is `false`, `totalSteps` is `0`. `TourEngine.send()` then calls `_renderCurrentStep()`, which returns early at `if (!step) return` (tour.ts:202), leaving `_active === true` with no popover, a stale spotlight, and no error, `tour:error` or warning. The user is stuck in an invisible tour that swallows arrow keys, and `nextStep()` from there reports the tour "complete".
findings.fix: Validate in `send()`: if `!(target in this._ctx.flow.states)` log/throw and return `false` without mutating state. Additionally, in `TourEngine._renderCurrentStep`, treat `!step` while `_active` as an error condition (`emit('tour:error')` + `_doEnd(false)`) rather than a silent return.
findings.verifierNote: machine.ts:79-85 verbatim — no membership check on `target`, unlike the constructor (16-20) and restore (140). Traced the aftermath: currentSteps falls back to `[]` (line 50), currentStep null (54), isFinal false (58), totalSteps 0 (62); TourEngine.send sees moved=true and non-final so calls _renderCurrentStep, which returns at `if (!step) return` (tour.ts:202) leaving _active true with no popover and no tour:error. Downgrading severity: this needs an authoring typo to trigger and produces a silent dead end rather than a shipped-broken default path — a notable robustness gap.

findings.title: Hint badge numbering restarts at 1 on every register() call, producing duplicate numbers; hint tooltips are never rendered
findings.impact: The badge label is derived from the index within the call, not from the number of already-mounted hints, so `gf.hints([a,b])` followed by `gf.hints([c,d])` renders badges 1,2,1,2 — and the accessible names collide too (`aria-label = \`Hint ${number}: ${step.hint}\``, line 124). Registering hints incrementally (per route, per lazily-mounted component) is the normal usage. Separately, `MountedHint.tooltipEl` is always `null` (line 153) and nothing ever creates the `.gf-hint-tooltip` element the CSS defines (lines 40-52), so `step.hint` is only exposed via `aria-label`: sighted users clicking a badge see no tooltip, only a `hint:click` event that — per hotspot-hint-events-never-forwarded — never reaches the instance.
findings.fix: Number from `this._hints.size + 1` inside the loop; either implement the tooltip element (created on mount, toggled on hover/focus/click like `HotspotManager._createTooltip`) or delete the unused CSS and drop `tooltipEl` from the type. Also give HintSystem/HotspotManager a real `destroy()` that calls `removeAllListeners()` — `createGuideFlow().destroy()` currently leaves their emitter listeners attached.
findings.verifierNote: hint.ts:83-86 verbatim — the badge number is `index + 1` within the current register() call, never derived from this._hints.size, so a second register() restarts at 1 for both the visible label (line 125) and the aria-label at line 124. Confirmed tooltipEl is hard-coded null at line 153 and grep shows '.gf-hint-tooltip' occurs only in the CSS block (line 40); no code creates that element, so step.hint reaches sighted users nowhere.

findings.title: IndexedDBDriver caches a rejected open promise forever and ignores blocked/versionchange events
findings.impact: A single failure of `indexedDB.open` — Firefox private browsing (open always fails), a transient `QuotaExceededError`, or a user clearing site data — permanently poisons `_dbPromise`; every later `get` returns `null` (silently) and every `set` logs a warning and drops the write, for the lifetime of the page. `openDB()` also has no `onblocked` handler, so if any other tab holds an older connection the promise never settles and every `await this._db()` hangs forever (each `get`/`set` awaits it), silently stalling `instance.start()`'s persistence checks. There is no `versionchange` handler either, so a future version bump in another tab blocks indefinitely, and `req.onupgradeneeded` calls `createObjectStore` unconditionally, which throws `ConstraintError` if the store already exists.
findings.fix: Clear the cache on failure (`this._dbPromise = openDB().catch(e => { this._dbPromise = null; throw e })`), add `req.onblocked` → reject with a timeout, add `db.onversionchange = () => { db.close(); this._dbPromise = null }`, guard the upgrade with `if (!req.result.objectStoreNames.contains(IDB_STORE_NAME))`, and reject on `tx.onabort`/`tx.onerror` (today only `req.onerror` is handled, so an aborted transaction leaves the promise pending).
findings.verifierNote: drivers.ts:63-68 verbatim, and the cached-rejection half is confirmed: a rejected _dbPromise is never reset, so every subsequent get returns null via the catch (line 80) and every set only warns (line 96) for the page lifetime. The rest does not hold at the current code: IDB_VERSION is pinned at 1 (line 48) and never bumped, so `onblocked` cannot fire and `onupgradeneeded` cannot re-run against an existing store — the never-settles hang and the ConstraintError are hypothetical future risks, not present defects. The driver is also opt-in (`persistence: { driver: 'indexedDB' }`), and the failure mode is silent degradation of persistence rather than a broken tour.
