findings.title: Prettier is configured with semi:false but half the source uses semicolons, and no script or CI step ever runs it
findings.evidence: "semi": false,
findings.impact: There is no `format` or `format:check` script anywhere — prettier appears only as a devDependency at package.json:36 — and no workflow runs it. Meanwhile the config's `"semi": false` is contradicted by every file in packages/ai, packages/analytics, packages/cli and packages/devtools (e.g. packages/ai/src/index.ts:29-40 and packages/cli/src/index.ts:22-31 are fully semicolon-terminated), while packages/core, react, svelte and vue are semicolon-free (packages/core/src/index.ts:19-27). The tsup configs split the same way: packages/ai/tsup.config.ts uses semicolons, packages/core/tsup.config.ts does not. So the moment anyone runs `prettier --write .`, it will reformat roughly half the repository and produce an unreviewable diff — and because no CI check exists, the divergence keeps growing.
findings.fix: Add `"format": "prettier --write ."` and `"format:check": "prettier --check ."` to the root package.json scripts, run `pnpm format` once as a single isolated commit, then add a `pnpm format:check` step to .github/workflows/ci.yml so the config is actually enforced.
findings.verifierNote: .prettierrc.json:2 is verbatim `"semi": false,`. Root package.json has no format or format:check script (scripts run lines 6-24; prettier appears only as a devDependency at line 36) and no workflow invokes it. The split is real: packages/ai/src/index.ts:29-40 and packages/cli/src/index.ts:22-31 are semicolon-terminated, while packages/core/src/index.ts:19-27 and packages/svelte/src/index.ts:18-19 are not; packages/ai/tsup.config.ts uses semicolons and packages/core/tsup.config.ts does not. P3 is correctly calibrated — cosmetic, no functional impact.

findings.title: apps/storybook's `test-storybook` script calls a binary that is not a dependency
findings.evidence: "test-storybook": "test-storybook"
findings.impact: The `test-storybook` binary is provided by `@storybook/test-runner`, which is absent from apps/storybook devDependencies (lines 10-25 list @storybook/addon-a11y, addon-essentials, addon-interactions, addon-links, react, react-vite, test, storybook — but not test-runner). Running `pnpm --filter storybook test-storybook` fails with command-not-found. Since the script is named `test-storybook` rather than `test`, `turbo run test` never touches it either, so the failure is invisible: the a11y addon (line 13) and the interaction-test addon (line 15) are configured in apps/storybook/.storybook/main.ts:7-9 but no runner ever executes their play functions or a11y checks.
findings.fix: Either add `"@storybook/test-runner": "^0.19.0"` to apps/storybook devDependencies and rename the script to `"test": "test-storybook"` so turbo picks it up (plus a CI job that boots storybook first), or delete the dead `test-storybook` script and the unused @storybook/addon-interactions/@storybook/test dependencies.
findings.verifierNote: apps/storybook/package.json:8 is verbatim `"test-storybook": "test-storybook"` and devDependencies at lines 10-25 list @types/react, @chromatic-com/storybook, addon-a11y, addon-essentials, addon-interactions, addon-links, react, react-vite, test, @vitejs/plugin-react, react, react-dom, storybook, vite — no @storybook/test-runner. addon-a11y and addon-interactions are registered at .storybook/main.ts:9 and :7. Severity lowered: this is a broken convenience script nobody runs — it is not wired into turbo (name is test-storybook, not test) or any workflow, so nothing regresses because of it.

findings.title: packages/svelte and packages/vue advertise "components" in their npm descriptions but ship none
findings.evidence: "description": "GuideFlow Svelte adapter — stores and components",
findings.impact: This description is what npmjs.com renders under the package name. packages/svelte/src/ contains exactly one file, index.ts, whose entire public surface is `createTourStore` plus type re-exports (packages/svelte/src/index.ts:62, :113-123) — there are no `.svelte` files, and tsup cannot compile them anyway, so "components" cannot be true. packages/vue/package.json:4 says "composables and components" while packages/vue/src/ holds only index.ts, plugin.ts and composables/use-tour.ts. A user shopping for a `<TourStep>` Svelte or Vue component installs the package and finds nothing, whereas @guideflow/react genuinely does ship four components (packages/react/src/index.ts:29-39). The docs pages are already honest — apps/docs/packages/svelte.md:18-22 lists only `createTourStore()` — so only the manifests mislead.
findings.fix: Change packages/svelte/package.json:4 to "GuideFlow Svelte adapter — reactive tour stores" and packages/vue/package.json:4 to "GuideFlow Vue 3 adapter — plugin and composables". Also drop `"tour-component"` from the svelte keywords (packages/svelte/package.json:15), since it advertises the same absent capability in npm search.
findings.verifierNote: packages/svelte/package.json:4 is verbatim `"description": "GuideFlow Svelte adapter — stores and components",` and packages/vue/package.json:4 says "composables and components". packages/svelte/src contains only index.ts (123 lines) exporting createTourStore at :62 plus type re-exports at :113-123 — no .svelte files. packages/vue/src contains only index.ts, plugin.ts and composables/use-tour.ts, matching the exports at index.ts:19-24. packages/react/src/index.ts:29-39 genuinely exports four components. apps/docs/packages/svelte.md:18-22 lists only createTourStore(), so the docs are honest and only the manifests overclaim.

findings.title: scripts/sync-repo-meta.mjs uses import.meta.dirname, which is undefined on Node 18 — below the repo's own engines floor
findings.evidence: const ROOT = resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..');
findings.impact: `import.meta.dirname` was added in Node 20.11.0 / 21.2.0. Root package.json:43 declares `"node": ">=18.0.0"` and README.md:562 tells contributors "Node.js ≥ 18", so a contributor on Node 18 running `pnpm sync-repo` (package.json:23) gets `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "path" argument must be of type string. Received undefined` from `resolve()` on the very first line of work. Nothing in CI runs this script (it is Node-22-only there), so the incompatibility is undetectable until a contributor hits it. There is also no .nvmrc to steer local Node versions toward the CI's Node 22.
findings.fix: Replace scripts/sync-repo-meta.mjs:13 with the portable form: `import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url'; const ROOT = resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..');` — the same pattern already used correctly in packages/cli/src/index.ts:34-35. Additionally add a `.nvmrc` containing `22` and raise `engines.node` to `>=20.11.0` if the newer syntax is preferred.
findings.verifierNote: scripts/sync-repo-meta.mjs:13 is verbatim `const ROOT = resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..');` and line 14 immediately calls `readFileSync(join(ROOT, ...))`, so the TypeError fires before any work. import.meta.dirname landed in Node 20.11.0/21.2.0. Root package.json:43 declares `"node": ">=18.0.0"`, README.md:562 says "Node.js ≥ 18", the script is exposed as `sync-repo` at package.json:23, and git ls-files confirms no .nvmrc. Severity lowered: this is a one-off maintenance utility run by hand, not part of build, test, CI or publish.

findings.title: turbo.json is Turbo-1.x-only (`pipeline`) and declares no `inputs` and no `env`/`globalEnv`, giving over-broad and env-blind cache keys
findings.impact: Three separate problems. (1) The `pipeline` key was renamed to `tasks` in Turbo 2; root package.json:38 pins `"turbo": "^1.13.2"` (lockfile resolves 1.13.4, the final 1.x), so any `pnpm up turbo` to 2.x makes every task fail with "Found `pipeline` field instead of `tasks`". (2) No task declares `inputs`, so editing packages/core/README.md or a `__tests__` file busts the `build` cache for core and cascades a rebuild through all six dependents. (3) `passThroughEnv: ["CI"]` appears on `test` (line 16) and `test:e2e` (line 21) but no task declares `env` and there is no `globalEnv`; under Turbo 1's default loose env mode, environment variables are not part of the hash at all, so a build produced with one `NODE_ENV`/`VITE_*` value is replayed for a different one. The `.next/**` outputs on line 7 are dead config — there is no Next.js app in the workspace.
findings.fix: Run `npx @turbo/codemod migrate` to rename `pipeline`→`tasks` and bump root package.json:38 to `"turbo": "^2"`. Add `"inputs": ["src/**", "tsup.config.ts", "package.json", "tsconfig.json"]` to `build`, `"inputs": ["src/**", "vitest.config.ts"]` to `test`, declare `"globalEnv": ["CI", "NODE_ENV"]`, add `"env": ["VITE_*"]` to the demo/devtools builds, and delete the `.next/**` output globs.
findings.verifierNote: All three facts check out: turbo.json:4 uses `pipeline` (renamed to `tasks` in Turbo 2), root package.json:38 pins `"turbo": "^1.13.2"`; no task declares `inputs`; passThroughEnv appears only on test (line 16) and test:e2e (line 21) with no `env`/`globalEnv`, and Turbo 1 loose mode does exclude undeclared env vars from the hash; and `.next/**` on line 7 is dead since apps/ holds only demo, docs, e2e, storybook. Downgraded because sub-claim (1) is a hypothetical about a future `pnpm up` rather than a current defect, and (2)/(3) cause cache inefficiency and theoretical staleness with no demonstrated wrong-output incident.

findings.title: No validate / doctor / record / dry-run commands, and no error taxonomy — every failure is exit code 1 with a raw dump
findings.impact: Four commands, no `validate` (nothing can check a FlowDefinition offline — see push-export-no-flow-validation), no `doctor` (nothing diagnoses missing peer deps, wrong Node version, or a broken install), no `record` (the README pitches recording tours but the CLI cannot), no `--dry-run` on the two commands that write/publish. Every failure path exits 1: file-not-found (export.ts:27, push.ts:32), bad JSON (push.ts:47), network failure (push.ts:76), and unhandled rejections all share one code, so scripts cannot distinguish "user typo" from "server down". The top-level handler prints the raw `err` object — for a `fetch` failure that is a multi-line Node `TypeError: fetch failed` with an opaque `cause`, not an actionable message. There is also no `.showHelpAfterError()` or `.showSuggestionAfterError()`, so a typo like `guideflow expor` prints a bare `error: unknown command` with no hint.
findings.fix: Add `program.showHelpAfterError().showSuggestionAfterError()` in index.ts. Introduce a small `CliError extends Error { code: number }` with distinct exit codes (2 usage, 3 not-found, 4 validation, 5 network, 6 auth), throw it from the commands instead of calling `process.exit` inline, and format it in the top-level catch (raw stack only under `--verbose`). Add `validate` (reuse the shared validator) and `doctor` as thin new `Command` files.
findings.verifierNote: index.ts:45-53 is verbatim and the structural claims hold: four addCommand calls, no validate/doctor/record, no --dry-run on export or push, every failure path (export.ts:27/44/56, push.ts:32/38/47/66/76 and the top-level catch) exits 1, and the program is built without .showHelpAfterError()/.showSuggestionAfterError(). One impact claim is false: 'the README pitches recording tours but the CLI cannot' — a case-insensitive grep for 'record' across README.md returns a single hit, line 411's `Record<string, boolean>` type. There is no recording pitch to contradict. Downgrading to P3: absent commands are a roadmap/scope opinion rather than a defect, the one substantive item (offline flow validation) is already captured by push-export-no-flow-validation, and undifferentiated exit codes in a four-command CLI are minor.

findings.title: studio's --port is parsed with parseInt and never validated, so a bad value silently becomes NaN
findings.evidence: const port = parseInt(opts.port, 10);
findings.impact: `guideflow studio --port abc` yields `NaN`, which is handed straight to Vite's `server.port`. The success message at line 42 then prints `Studio running at http://localhost:NaN` — a URL the user cannot open — while the server is actually listening on some other port. `parseInt('3000abc')` likewise yields `3000` with no warning, and there is no range check (a port of `70000` or `-1` reaches Vite unchecked).
findings.fix: Validate after parsing: `if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65535) { console.error(...); process.exit(1); }`, or use Commander's option parser argument (`.option('-p, --port <port>', '...', parsePort, 4747)`) so the error surfaces during argument parsing.
findings.verifierNote: Line 17 `const port = parseInt(opts.port, 10);` is verbatim and there is genuinely no NaN/range check, and `parseInt('3000abc') === 3000` silently is real. But the central impact assertion is wrong. I tested it: `http.createServer().listen(NaN)` throws ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT ('options.port should be >= 0 and < 65536. Received type number (NaN).') synchronously, so Vite's httpServerStart rejects, studio.ts's catch at line 49 fires, and the user sees `Failed to start Studio` plus that message — line 42's success line never runs. Nothing prints 'http://localhost:NaN' and nothing listens on another port. Same for 70000 and -1: Node rejects them rather than accepting them 'unchecked'. What remains is a poor error message and silent truncation of '3000abc' — P3.

findings.title: README claims studio "opens browser" but the server is created with open:false
findings.evidence: | `guideflow studio` | Launch the visual tour editor (opens browser) |
findings.impact: `studio.ts:26` passes `server: { open: false }`, and nothing else in the command shells out to a browser opener. The user is left staring at `Studio running at http://localhost:4747` and must open it manually. There is also no `--open` flag to get the documented behaviour, and no `--host` flag for container/WSL use.
findings.fix: Either add `-o, --open` (wired to Vite's `server.open`) and default it to true to match the docs, or strike "(opens browser)" from README.md:534. Add `--host` while touching this.
findings.verifierNote: README.md:534 verbatim `| \`guideflow studio\` | Launch the visual tour editor (opens browser) |`, and studio.ts:26 passes `server: { port, open: false }`. Nothing else in the command opens a browser, and the only options declared are -p/--port and --root (lines 14-15) — no --open, no --host. apps/docs/api/cli.md:67 hedges correctly ('Opens the Studio at http://localhost:4747') but the README table does not.

findings.title: studio's SIGINT handler exits before the server finishes closing, and there is no SIGTERM handler
findings.impact: `server.close()` returns a Promise that is discarded via `void`, then `process.exit(0)` runs synchronously on the same tick, so open sockets, file watchers and the HMR websocket are torn down by process death rather than cleanly. On Windows in particular this can leave the port in a lingering state so an immediate re-run of `guideflow studio` fails with EADDRINUSE. There is no `SIGTERM` handler at all, so `docker stop` / process-manager shutdown skips cleanup entirely.
findings.fix: Make the handler async and await the close: `const shutdown = async () => { await server.close(); process.exit(0); };` registered for both `'SIGINT'` and `'SIGTERM'`.
findings.verifierNote: studio.ts:45-48 is verbatim: the close() promise is discarded via `void` and process.exit(0) runs on the same tick, and there is no SIGTERM (or SIGHUP) handler anywhere in the file. So the defect is real. The stated impact is unproven, though: process death closes listening sockets and Node sets SO_REUSEADDR on listen, so a lingering-port EADDRINUSE on Windows is speculative — I could not reproduce or find evidence for it. The practical consequence of skipping a graceful close on a dev server that is being killed anyway is small, and the SIGTERM gap only matters in a containerised studio, which nothing here documents. Downgrading to P3.

findings.title: LocalStorageDriver.remove()/keys() are unguarded — a storage SecurityError rejects start() and the tour never opens
findings.impact: `isBrowser()` only checks `window`/`document`; it says nothing about storage availability. Accessing `localStorage` throws `SecurityError` when cookies/site data are blocked (Safari with "block all cookies", Chrome third-party/partitioned iframe contexts, some enterprise policies). `get`/`set` wrap that in try/catch, but `remove` and `keys` do not. `ProgressStore.loadSnapshot` calls `remove` on any expired entry (progress-store.ts:50) and `isDismissed` does the same (line 77) — both are awaited inside `instance.start()` (index.ts:245-248), so the throw rejects the `start()` promise and no tour renders at all; `resetUser` throws for the same reason. In an iframe with storage blocked this turns a cosmetic degradation into a total feature outage plus an unhandled promise rejection.
findings.fix: Wrap `remove`/`keys` in try/catch like `get`/`set`, and add a one-time availability probe (`try { localStorage.setItem('__gf', '1'); localStorage.removeItem('__gf') } catch { available = false }`) so the driver degrades to a no-op in-memory shim. Independently, wrap the persistence block in `instance.start()` in try/catch so a storage failure can never prevent a tour from starting.
findings.verifierNote: drivers.ts:32-40 is verbatim and isBrowser (utils/ssr.ts:6-7) indeed only checks window/document, so remove()/keys() are genuinely unguarded. But the stated impact does not hold: ProgressStore.loadSnapshot only calls remove after `get` returned a truthy entry (progress-store.ts:47-51) and isDismissed likewise (74-78) — if localStorage access throws, `get`'s try/catch (drivers.ts:18-20) returns null and the remove branch is never reached. So start() (index.ts:245-248) cannot reject from this path. The only reachable throw is `keys()` via resetUser (progress-store.ts:126-129), which core never calls. Real but minor inconsistency, not a feature outage.

findings.title: Bridge reads gf.version, which core does not expose, so the panel header renders "vunknown"
findings.evidence: payload: { version: gf.version ?? 'unknown' },
findings.impact: `GuideFlowInstance` (packages/core/src/index.ts:94-140) declares no `version` member and `createGuideFlow` never assigns one, so `gf.version` is always `undefined` and the payload is the literal string `'unknown'`. The panel then does `if (pl?.version) setVersion(pl.version)` (app.tsx:1142-1143) — `'unknown'` is truthy — and renders `v{version}` (line 1197), so the header permanently shows a monospace badge reading `vunknown` next to the green detected dot. It looks like a rendering bug and gives the user no version information for the one thing the badge exists to report.
findings.fix: Add a `readonly version: string` to `GuideFlowInstance` populated from the package version at build time, and in the panel treat `'unknown'` as absent (`if (pl?.version && pl.version !== 'unknown')`) so the badge is hidden rather than showing a placeholder.
findings.verifierNote: bridge.ts:87 is `payload: { version: gf.version ?? 'unknown' }` (cited as :88, off by one). packages/core/src/index.ts declares no `version` member on GuideFlowInstance (interface at 89-141) and grep for 'version' in that file returns nothing, so it is always undefined. app.tsx:1142 `if (pl?.version)` passes on the truthy string and 1197 renders `v{version}` → 'vunknown'. Downgrading to P3: cosmetic badge text, no functional loss.

findings.title: Rollup is configured with a single ES output format, so the content script would break the moment it gains an import
findings.impact: No `format` is specified, so Vite's default (`es`) applies to every entry — including `content`, which Chrome loads as a *classic* script. Today `dist/content.js` happens to contain zero `import`/`export` statements only because `inspector.ts` imports nothing; the moment anyone imports a shared helper (or Rollup decides to hoist a chunk shared with `bridge`), the content script gets `import { x } from './chunks/…'` and dies at load with `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module`, taking element picking, recording, and detection with it. The same trap applies to `bridge.js`: `web_accessible_resources` lists only `["bridge.js"]` (manifest.json:32), so any chunk it imports would be blocked as a non-web-accessible resource. A single-output-format Rollup config structurally cannot produce the IIFE content script MV3 needs.
findings.fix: Split the build into two Vite invocations (or use `@crxjs/vite-plugin`): one with `build.rollupOptions.output.format: 'iife'`, `inlineDynamicImports: true` for the `content` and `bridge` entries, and the current ES build for `panel`/`popup`/`background`. Add `"chunks/*.js"` to `web_accessible_resources` if the bridge is ever allowed to code-split. Add a post-build assertion that `dist/content.js` contains no top-level `import`.
findings.verifierNote: vite.config.ts:89-94 verbatim and no `format` is set, so ES output applies. But I checked the actual build: dist/content.js and dist/bridge.js contain zero import/export statements today (grep count 0 on both), and the only emitted chunk (dist/chunks/client-CTQ0Ju4c.js) is consumed by panel.js/popup.js, which are extension pages loaded as modules. So nothing is broken as shipped — this is a latent structural risk contingent on a future edit. P3.

findings.title: contextMenus.create on every onInstalled throws duplicate-id errors when the extension updates
findings.impact: `onInstalled` fires with reason `"update"` as well as `"install"`, and context menu items registered by an extension persist across updates. Creating an item with an existing id raises `Cannot create item with duplicate id gf-add-element`, surfaced as an unchecked `chrome.runtime.lastError` in the worker. Separately, all three items use `contexts: ['all']` with no page filtering, so they appear in the right-click menu of every page in the browser regardless of whether GuideFlow is present — and "Add Element to GuideFlow Tour" / "Quick Tour from Here" do nothing at all unless the DevTools panel happens to be open, because `GF_ELEMENT_SELECTED`/`GF_QUICK_TOUR_ELEMENT` are only routed to `devtoolsPorts` (service-worker.ts:150-153). "Quick Tour from Here" also never creates or starts a tour — the panel handler just sets the selected element and switches tabs (app.tsx:1165-1170).
findings.fix: Call `chrome.contextMenus.removeAll(() => { /* create items */ })` inside the `onInstalled` listener. Buffer context-menu captures in `chrome.storage.session` so they survive until a panel opens, and either implement "Quick Tour from Here" (build and start a one-step flow) or rename it to match what it does.
findings.verifierNote: service-worker.ts:45-61 verbatim — three unconditional creates in onInstalled with no `chrome.contextMenus.removeAll()` first, and no callback checking runtime.lastError. onInstalled does fire with reason 'update', and menu registrations survive updates, so the duplicate-id error is real. The bundled sub-claims also check out: all three use contexts:['all'] with no documentUrlPatterns, and GF_ELEMENT_SELECTED/GF_QUICK_TOUR_ELEMENT only reach devtoolsPorts (149-153), with app.tsx:1165-1170 merely setting the selected element. Downgrading to P3: the failure is an unchecked lastError in the worker log; the menus themselves keep working.

findings.title: Panel never clears detected/flows/version when the inspected page navigates away from GuideFlow
findings.impact: `setDetected(false)` is never called anywhere in the file, and there is no `chrome.devtools.network.onNavigated` listener. Navigate the inspected tab from a GuideFlow page to any other page and the panel keeps the green dot, the version badge, the stale `flows` list, and the stale `selectedElement` — whose selector now points at an element that no longer exists. Clicking ▶ Run on a stale flow silently does nothing (the bridge's `if (!gf) return`). The Events log also accumulates across navigations with no page-boundary marker, so events from two different pages are interleaved with no way to tell them apart.
findings.fix: Register `chrome.devtools.network.onNavigated.addListener(url => { setDetected(false); setVersion(null); setFlows([]); setSelectedElement(null); appendNavigationMarker(url); sendToContent({ type: 'GF_DEVTOOLS_OPEN' }); })` so the panel re-probes and shows an honest state after every navigation.
findings.verifierNote: Grep of app.tsx for setDetected returns only the declaration (1031) and `setDetected(true)` (1140); `onNavigated` appears nowhere. So detected/version/flows/selectedElement all persist across navigations, and events accumulate with no page boundary (1145-1148). The bridge's `if (!gf) return` at bridge.ts:129 does make a stale Run a silent no-op as described.

findings.title: Events tab force-scrolls to the bottom on every incoming event with no pause control
findings.impact: The effect fires on every `events` change regardless of scroll position, so a user scrolled up to read an earlier `tour:error` is yanked back to the bottom the instant the next event arrives — and `behavior: 'smooth'` makes each yank a visible animation. During an active tour, events arrive several per step, making the log effectively unreadable. There is no autoscroll toggle, no "stick to bottom only when already at bottom" check, and no pause/record control on the log at all. The 500-event cap (`prev.slice(-499)`, line 1147) silently drops older events with no indication that truncation occurred.
findings.fix: Only scroll when the container is already within ~40px of the bottom, add an explicit "Auto-scroll" toggle and a pause button in the Events toolbar, and render a "showing last 500 events (older dropped)" notice when the cap is hit.
findings.verifierNote: app.tsx:724-726 verbatim — the effect depends on `events` with no at-bottom check, no toggle, and behavior:'smooth'. The 500-cap via `prev.slice(-499)` at line 1147 is also as described, with no truncation indicator in the EventsTab render (786-812).

findings.title: GF_HIGHLIGHT_SELECTOR passes user-authored strings straight to querySelector with no try/catch
findings.impact: Selectors reach this path from imported JSON (app.tsx:481 `setSteps(data.steps)` with zero validation) and from steps the user edits by hand. An invalid selector makes `document.querySelector` throw `SyntaxError: Failed to execute 'querySelector'`, which escapes the `chrome.runtime.onMessage` listener uncaught. There is also no feedback when the selector is *valid but matches nothing* — the 👁 Preview button (app.tsx:685-691) simply does nothing, giving the user no way to distinguish "selector is wrong" from "button is broken", which is the single most important signal a visual tour builder owes its user.
findings.fix: Wrap in try/catch and reply with a `GF_HIGHLIGHT_RESULT` message carrying `{ ok, matchCount, error }`; render it in the panel next to the step (green check / "0 matches" / "invalid selector"). Validate imported step targets on import with the same call.
findings.verifierNote: inspector.ts:337-339 verbatim; no try/catch, and app.tsx:481 does `setSteps(data.steps)` with no validation. An invalid selector does throw SyntaxError out of the onMessage listener. Downgrading to P3: the throw is contained to that one listener invocation (subsequent messages still dispatch), so the observable impact is a console error plus the pre-existing 'no feedback on zero matches' UX gap.

findings.title: Inspect mode swallows all clicks with no Escape key handler, and the popup closes itself after starting it
findings.impact: While inspecting, every click on the page is cancelled — links, buttons, and forms all stop working. There is no `keydown`/Escape listener anywhere in inspector.ts, so the only exits are picking an element or reloading the page. The popup makes this a trap: `handlePickElement` sends `GF_START_INSPECT` and then calls `window.close()` (popup.tsx:291-292), so a user who clicks Pick Element by accident has no visible control anywhere to cancel — the popup is gone and the DevTools panel may not be open. Unlike recording, inspect mode shows no on-page badge at all, so there is no visual indication of why the page stopped responding to clicks.
findings.fix: Add `document.addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'Escape') { stopInspect(); send({ type: 'GF_INSPECT_STOPPED' }); } }, true)` in `startInspect`, and render an on-page cancel affordance (reuse the recording-badge pattern) so inspect mode is always visibly escapable.
findings.verifierNote: Verified there is no keydown/Escape listener anywhere in inspector.ts (grep returns nothing) and popup.tsx:291-292 does close the popup after GF_START_INSPECT. But the trap claim is overstated: onClick calls `stopInspect()` at inspector.ts:276 before sending, so inspect mode exits on the very first click — only one click is swallowed, not 'every click on the page' until reload. The residual defect is a spurious element selection plus no visible mode indicator. P3.

findings.title: Panel and popup hardcode a dark palette and ignore chrome.devtools.panels.themeName
findings.evidence:
root: {
    display: 'grid' as const,
    gridTemplateRows: 'auto 1fr',
    height: '100%',
    background: '#1e1e2e',
    color: '#cdd6f4',
findings.impact: Every colour in both UIs is a literal Catppuccin Mocha hex value. `chrome.devtools.panels.themeName` (`'default'` | `'dark'`) is never read, and there is no `prefers-color-scheme` media query anywhere in the package. A user running DevTools in the light theme gets a dark slab wedged between light panels — visually jarring and, more importantly, the low-contrast greys chosen for a dark surround (`#6c7086` on `#1e1e2e` for all secondary label text, `#585b70` on `#181825` for step bodies at line 705) sit near or below the WCAG AA 4.5:1 threshold and are unreadable for anyone with reduced contrast sensitivity. The popup is equally locked to dark regardless of OS theme.
findings.fix: Read `chrome.devtools.panels.themeName` on mount, expose the palette as CSS custom properties on `:root`, and provide a light variant; add a `@media (prefers-color-scheme: light)` fallback for the popup. Raise the secondary text colours to meet 4.5:1 against their actual backgrounds.
findings.verifierNote: app.tsx:54-59 hardcodes background '#1e1e2e'/color '#cdd6f4' (cited as :57, a few lines off; content verbatim). Grep for themeName and prefers-color-scheme across packages/devtools/src returns zero hits, and popup.tsx:26-217 is likewise literal hex throughout. I computed the contrast for #6c7086 on #1e1e2e: ~3.4:1, below the 4.5:1 AA threshold, so the readability claim holds.

findings.title: Popup hardcodes version v0.2.0 while the manifest, package, and panel all say 0.1.9
findings.evidence: v0.2.0
findings.impact: manifest.json:4 is `"version": "0.1.9"`, package.json:3 is `"version": "0.1.9"`, and the panel's About card renders `Extension v0.1.9` (app.tsx:1018) — also hardcoded. The popup shows `v0.2.0` in two places (line 345 and the footer at line 498). All four strings are manual literals that will drift on every release, and a user filing a bug report will cite whichever number they happened to see. The popup footer also links to `https://guideflow.dev`, a domain that appears nowhere else in the repo (all other links point at github.com/RealNerdZW/GuideFlow).
findings.fix: Replace all four literals with `chrome.runtime.getManifest().version`, which is available in both the popup and the panel. Point the Docs link at the actual published docs URL used by apps/docs, or remove it.
findings.verifierNote: popup.tsx:345 and :498 both say v0.2.0; manifest.json:4 and package.json:3 are 0.1.9 and app.tsx:1018 hardcodes 'Extension v0.1.9'. One sub-claim is wrong: guideflow.dev does appear elsewhere — apps/demo/src/App.tsx:178/783/843 reference api.guideflow.dev. Downgrading to P3: purely a cosmetic string drift.

findings.title: autoInit() routes attribute tours through the deprecated `guideflow` proxy and is documented nowhere
findings.evidence: const instance = config ? createGuideFlow(config) : guideflow
findings.impact: autoInit() — the intended zero-config entry point for the Intro.js compatibility layer and script-tag users — falls back to the `guideflow` export that the file itself marks @deprecated at line 355 and whose Proxy set trap silently discards writes. It is exported from packages/core/src/index.ts:382 but appears in no VitePress page, no README section, and no migration guide, so the compat path most likely to attract migrating Intro.js users is both undiscoverable and built on a deprecated primitive. It also has no return value and no way to obtain the instance it created.
findings.fix: Change the fallback to getGuideFlow(), return the created instance from autoInit(), and document it on apps/docs/guide/migrate-intro.md as the supported drop-in entry point.

findings.title: GuidanceContext.featureFlags is a published API surface that no code in core, the adapters, or the docs ever reads
findings.evidence: featureFlags?: Record<string, boolean>
findings.impact: featureFlags is exported in the public .d.ts and implies a feature-flag integration story, but the only places it is ever touched are an intro-compat doc comment, an intro-compat unit test, and apps/demo/src/main.tsx:25. Nothing in TourEngine, createGuideFlow, ProgressStore, or any adapter reads it; it is reachable only if the user happens to write `showIf: ctx => ctx.featureFlags?.x`. There is no LaunchDarkly/Statsig/Unleash/OpenFeature adapter, no docs page, and no way to flag-gate a whole flow rather than a step. Users will reasonably assume flag-driven targeting works and find it does nothing.
findings.fix: Either wire it into a flow-level gate (`FlowDefinition.requiresFlag`) evaluated in createGuideFlow's start(), and document an OpenFeature-shaped provider hook, or remove the field from GuidanceContext so the type stops advertising capability that does not exist.

findings.title: The project markets a hosted Cloud product while shipping MIT everywhere with no pricing, no CLA, and a LICENSE naming the wrong GitHub account
findings.evidence: Copyright (c) 2026 John Mugabe (https://github.com/johnmugabe)
findings.impact: README.md advertises 'push to GuideFlow Cloud' and the CLI defaults to api.guideflow.dev, but there is no pricing page, no terms, no dual-licence or BSL arrangement, no CLA, and no statement of what is open-source versus commercial. The LICENSE additionally credits github.com/johnmugabe while repo.config.json declares owner RealNerdZW and every package.json uses github.com/RealNerdZW — an ownership ambiguity that a legal reviewer at an adopting company will flag. There is no CODEOWNERS, no governance doc, and no maintainer-count statement, so the bus-factor and sustainability questions every adoption review asks have no answer.
findings.fix: Fix the LICENSE copyright URL to match repo.config.json (and extend scripts/sync-repo-meta.mjs to cover LICENSE), then state the commercial posture explicitly in README.md — either 'fully MIT, no hosted product planned' or a clear open-core boundary — and add CODEOWNERS.

findings.title: apps/docs/public/sitemap.xml is hand-written with 6 URLs for a 57-page site and is never regenerated
findings.evidence: <loc>https://realnerdzw.github.io/GuideFlow/</loc>
findings.impact: The file lists 6 <url> entries (root, guide/, api/, themes/, and two others) while the VitePress sidebar resolves 57 distinct pages, all of which exist. robots.txt points crawlers at this sitemap as authoritative. Every guide page, API reference page, and theme page beyond the four section indexes is therefore absent from the declared sitemap, and because the file is static in public/ it will never pick up new pages. For a project whose only distribution channel is organic discovery of its docs, this silently suppresses indexing of ~90% of the content — and the docs' own frontmatter is heavily SEO-tuned, so the omission is clearly unintended.
findings.fix: Replace the static file with VitePress's built-in `sitemap: { hostname }` config in apps/docs/.vitepress/config.ts, which generates entries for every built page, and delete apps/docs/public/sitemap.xml.

findings.title: guideflow studio starts an unauthenticated Vite dev server rooted at an arbitrary user-supplied directory
findings.impact: `--root` is passed through `resolve()` with no containment check and handed directly to Vite as the serving root, so `guideflow studio --root /` (or `--root ~`, or `--root ../..`) turns the entire filesystem below that point into an HTTP-readable tree on port 4747 with no authentication, no token, and no allowlist — requests for paths such as `/Users/me/.aws/credentials` or `.ssh/id_rsa` become reachable by every local process and every other user on a shared or terminal-server host. There is also no `server.host` pin: the command inherits Vite's default rather than explicitly binding loopback, so a config file or `--host` in the project's own vite config can expose it on the LAN, and no `server.cors`/`server.origin` policy is set, leaving the dev server's default permissive CORS and the well-known dev-server WebSocket-origin weaknesses in play against a developer who visits a hostile page while Studio is running. `parseInt(opts.port, 10)` is also unvalidated — `--port abc` yields `NaN`, which Vite resolves to an arbitrary port that the success message at line 42 then misreports.
findings.fix: Reject roots outside the project: resolve `opts.root` and require that it be inside `process.cwd()`, or at minimum refuse `/` and the user's home directory. Pin the binding and tighten the surface explicitly: `server: { port, host: '127.0.0.1', strictPort: true, open: false, cors: false, fs: { strict: true, allow: [root] } }`. Validate the port (`Number.isInteger(port) && port > 0 && port < 65536`). Consider requiring a per-session token in the URL so a hostile page cannot blind-address the server.
findings.verifierNote: studio.ts:16-26 is verbatim and --root does default to '.' (line 15) and is passed to createServer with no containment check. But this is the ordinary contract of every dev server: the operator chooses the root, running with their own privileges — `guideflow studio --root /` is the user aiming at their own foot, not a boundary an attacker crosses. The host claim is also wrong in the auditor's favour and then walked back: Vite's server.host default is already loopback, so nothing is exposed to the LAN unless the project's own vite config opts in, and this command sets no --host flag at all. The only independently verifiable defect is the unvalidated `parseInt(opts.port, 10)` at line 17 producing NaN, which line 42 then misreports. Downgrading to P3.

findings.title: Bridge broadcasts every tour event to the page with postMessage(msg, "*"), letting any third-party script on the page read all tour data
findings.impact: Every GuideFlow event payload — plus the full registered flow list at lines 96-99 (`window.postMessage({ source: BRIDGE_SOURCE, type: 'GF_FLOWS_LIST', payload: flows }, '*')`) and the version at lines 83-90 — is broadcast to the page's own message bus with a `*` target origin. Any script sharing the page (an analytics tag, an ad script, a compromised npm dependency, an injected browser extension) registers a `message` listener filtering on `e.data?.source === '__gf_bridge__'` and silently exfiltrates the complete tour definitions and event stream — which routinely contain internal feature-flag names, unreleased-feature copy, admin-only step targets, and any `meta` fields the app attached. Forgery is symmetric: because the content script's inbound filter is the same public string constant, a page script can also inject a fabricated `GF_FLOWS_LIST` that the DevTools panel renders as legitimate "Page Flows" (packages/devtools/src/panel/app.tsx:1150-1152 `setFlows(msg.payload as unknown[])`) and offers a Run button for (app.tsx:899 `onClick={() => sendToContent({ type: 'GF_START_TOUR', payload: f })}`), so the developer is socially engineered into executing an attacker-supplied flow payload. Note the inbound guard at bridge.ts:126 (`if (data?.source !== CONTENT_SOURCE) return;`) provides no protection either — `'__gf_content__'` is equally public — though forging that direction is not an escalation since a page script can already call `window.__guideflow.start()` directly in its own world.
findings.fix: Stop using the shared page message bus. Create the channel once during injection: in inspector.ts, construct a `MessageChannel` and transfer `port2` to the bridge in a single origin-targeted init message, so no other page script holds a reference. At minimum, replace `'*'` with `window.location.origin` on all four `postMessage` calls (bridge.ts:83, 96, 111, 144, 167) — that does not stop same-origin page scripts but removes cross-origin frame leakage — and only relay tour data once the panel has actually connected, rather than broadcasting unconditionally from `tryRelay()`.
findings.verifierNote: The quoted code at bridge.ts:108-115 is verbatim, as are the '*' targets at 96-99 and 83-90. But the headline impact does not hold: bridge.js is injected into the PAGE world (inspector.ts:41-51, `script.src = chrome.runtime.getURL('bridge.js')` appended to the page), so everything it broadcasts it obtained from `window.__guideflow` — a global any script sharing the page can already read directly via `gf.listFlows()` and `gf.on(...)`. No privilege or origin boundary is crossed by the postMessage, so 'silently exfiltrates data a third-party script could not otherwise get' is wrong. The residual real concern is the inbound-forgery path into the panel (fabricated GF_FLOWS_LIST rendered at app.tsx:1150-1151 with a Run button at 899) — but that is the same root cause already charged in devtools-content-script-relays-any-message-type, and the auditor concedes the CONTENT_SOURCE direction is not an escalation. Downgrading to P3 as a hardening nit.

findings.title: watchAttributeTour auto-adopts data-gf-* attributes from dynamically injected DOM, turning HTML-attribute injection into branded in-app phishing
findings.evidence: obs.observe(target, { childList: true, subtree: true, attributes: true, attributeFilter: [ATTR_STEP] })
findings.impact: `watchAttributeTour` observes `document.body` by default (line 118: `const target = root ?? document.body`) with `subtree: true`, and on any mutation re-scans and invokes the caller's `callback(flow)` — which the documented usage wires to starting a tour. `scanAttributeTour` picks up any element carrying `data-gf-step` and lifts `data-gf-title`/`data-gf-body` into step content (lines 42-84). So on a page that renders user-supplied HTML — a rich-text comment, a markdown field, a shared document title — an attacker who can only inject attributes (a scenario many sanitizers explicitly permit, since `data-*` attributes are inert to them) can inject `<div data-gf-step="1" data-gf-title="Session expired" data-gf-body="Confirm your password to continue">` and cause the host app to spontaneously display attacker-authored copy inside GuideFlow's own `role="dialog" aria-modal="true"` popover, styled with the application's real branding at z-index 999999. `data-gf-step` is parsed with `parseInt` for ordering, so `data-gf-step="0"` places the fake step first. The content itself is escaped by `_esc` (default-renderer.ts:174, 178), so this is not script execution — it is high-credibility UI redress/phishing, which is the more effective attack for credential capture. To be explicit about what is not wrong here: the `data-gf-show-if` evaluator (lines 49-72) is correctly implemented — gated by `/^[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$.]*$/`, performing a read-only dot-path walk and returning `!!current` — so it is not eval-like and cannot pollute prototypes; the only nit is that the regex admits `__proto__`/`constructor` segments, which is harmless for reads.
findings.fix: Scope the observer: make the `root` parameter required rather than defaulting to `document.body`, so an integrator must opt a specific trusted container in. Add an `allowlist`/`filter` option so callers can reject elements that fail an app-specific trust check. Document prominently in apps/docs/guide/migrate-intro.md that `data-gf-*` attributes are treated as trusted tour-authoring input and must never be reachable from user-generated content, and tighten the `showIf` path regex to reject `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` segments for defence in depth.
findings.verifierNote: intro-compat.ts:137 is verbatim, target defaults to document.body at line 118, and when root is undefined line 130's scanAttributeTour(root) falls through to `const container = root ?? document` at line 30 — so the whole document is rescanned and callback(flow) fired, despite the comment at 129 claiming scoping. scanAttributeTour does lift data-gf-title/body into content (42-84) and sorts by parseInt of data-gf-step. The auditor's exculpatory notes are also accurate: the show-if evaluator at 49-72 is gated by /^[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$.]*$/ and is a read-only walk, and content is escaped by _esc at default-renderer.ts:174/178, so this is not script execution. Downgrading to P3: the attack requires the host app to opt into watchAttributeTour AND to have a separate attribute-injection hole, and the payoff is UI redress only.

findings.title: Every published package ships its src/ directory, disclosing source and doubling install size
findings.evidence:
"files": [
    "dist",
    "src",
    "README.md"
  ],
findings.impact: All seven publishable packages (core, react, vue, svelte, ai, analytics, cli — verified identical `files` arrays) ship `src/` alongside `dist/`. Consequences: (a) consumers download roughly twice the necessary bytes on every install, and bundlers that resolve by directory can pick up the un-transpiled TypeScript; (b) the raw source of the security-sensitive code is published to the npm CDN, so an attacker studying the `_sanitizeHTML` denylist or the devtools sentinel constants does not even need to unminify a bundle; (c) anything accidentally left in `src/` — a scratch file, a fixture containing a real token, a commented-out internal endpoint — is published irrevocably, and since there is no `.npmignore` anywhere in the repo there is no second line of defence. Sourcemaps are the correct mechanism for the debugging benefit this is presumably meant to provide.
findings.fix: Remove `"src"` from the `files` array in packages/{core,react,vue,svelte,ai,analytics,cli}/package.json, leaving `["dist", "README.md"]`. Enable `sourcemap: true` in each tsup.config.ts so consumers still get readable stack traces without shipping source. Add an `npm pack --dry-run` review step (or the `publint` / `arethetypeswrong` checks) to ci.yml so future `files` regressions are caught.
findings.verifierNote: I read the files array from all seven package.json files programmatically — core, react, vue, svelte, ai, analytics and cli all return exactly ["dist","src","README.md"] — and confirmed no .npmignore exists under packages/. Downgrading to P3: consequence (b) is not a real security consequence, since npm tarballs are public by definition and dist is trivially readable regardless of whether src ships; (c) is a hypothetical about files that do not exist in the tree. What remains verified is roughly doubled install size and the loss of a second line of defence — a minor packaging hygiene issue.
